title: Preparing for Surgery

en.description: What to expect before, during, and after your child's anesthesia for surgery, and when to call for help.

content.markdown:
At Mass General Brigham for Children, our pediatric surgery team delivers high-quality surgical care for infants, children, and young adults. Our top pediatric surgeons specialize in pediatric general surgery and thoracic surgery, treating everything from common problems like a hernia or appendicitis to complex congenital conditions of the abdomen or chest.

### Pediatric Surgery

- 📞 [617-726-0270](tel:+16177260270)
- 🌐 [massgeneralbrigham.org/en/services/pediatric-surgery](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/en/services/pediatric-surgery)

Children who need anesthesia or sedation for medical tests, procedures, or surgery receive expert care from our pediatric anesthesia team. We focus on your child's safety, comfort, and pain relief before, during, and after care.

## What to expect before your child gets anesthesia

Your child's care team will provide instructions about eating, drinking, and medication use before anesthesia.

You will meet with a member of the pediatric anesthesia team before the procedure. This is a good time to:

- Ask questions and share any concerns
- Provide a complete medical history, including allergies, medications, and supplements
- Share your child's past experiences with anesthesia
- Let us know about a family history of anesthesia complications or neuromuscular conditions, such as muscular dystrophy

## What to expect during anesthesia

You may be able to stay with your child while they are prepared for anesthesia, and sometimes until they fall asleep. Talking calmly or helping your child focus on something familiar can be reassuring.

As anesthesia begins, your child may:

- Roll their eyes upward
- Seem restless and move around
- Snore or make funny noises

These reactions are normal and usually last less than a minute. Although your child may seem awake, they will not remember this part of the experience.

## Recovery after anesthesia

After the procedure, your child will wake up in a recovery area where they are closely monitored. Recovery time varies, but many children stay for up to three hours.

During recovery, your child may:

- Seem confused or restless or not recognize you
- Feel nauseated or vomit
- Need pain or anti-nausea medication

These effects are common and usually temporary. A care team member will explain what to expect and when your child is ready to go home.

## At-home recovery and safety

After your child's procedure, you should follow the care team's instructions. You may need to:

- Keep your child resting and supervised
- Offer clear liquids and avoid heavy meals
- Help your child sleep on their side
- Limit physical activity for the rest of the day

For older children and teens, driving, alcohol, smoking, and vaping should be avoided after anesthesia.

## When to call for help

You should call your child's care team if your child has:

- A bad headache or pain
- Nausea or vomiting that lasts more than four hours
- Trouble drinking fluids or has not urinated for 12 hours
- Excessive sleepiness or restlessness

Call 9-1-1 or go to the nearest emergency room if your child:

- Can't wake up from sleep
- Has pale, gray, or blue skin
- Has slow or shallow breathing

es.description: Qué esperar antes, durante y después de la anestesia de su hijo para la cirugía, y cuándo llamar para pedir ayuda.

content.markdown:
En Mass General Brigham for Children, nuestro equipo de cirugía pediátrica brinda atención quirúrgica de alta calidad a bebés, niños y adultos jóvenes. Nuestros principales cirujanos pediátricos se especializan en cirugía general pediátrica y cirugía torácica, y tratan desde problemas comunes, como hernias o apendicitis, hasta afecciones congénitas complejas del abdomen o el pecho.

### Cirugía Pediátrica

- 📞 [617-726-0270](tel:+16177260270)
- 🌐 [massgeneralbrigham.org/es/services/pediatric-surgery](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/es/services/pediatric-surgery)

Los niños que necesitan anestesia o sedación para pruebas médicas, procedimientos o cirugía reciben atención experta de nuestro equipo de anestesia pediátrica. Nos enfocamos en la seguridad, comodidad y alivio del dolor de su hijo antes, durante y después de la atención.

## Qué esperar antes de que su hijo reciba anestesia

El equipo de atención de su hijo proporcionará instrucciones sobre la alimentación, la bebida y el uso de medicamentos antes de la anestesia.

Se reunirá con un miembro del equipo de anestesia pediátrica antes del procedimiento. Este es un buen momento para:

- Hacer preguntas y compartir cualquier inquietud
- Proporcionar un historial médico completo, incluyendo alergias, medicamentos y suplementos
- Compartir las experiencias pasadas de su hijo con la anestesia
- Informarnos sobre antecedentes familiares de complicaciones con la anestesia o afecciones neuromusculares, como la distrofia muscular

## Qué esperar durante la anestesia

Puede que pueda quedarse con su hijo mientras lo preparan para la anestesia, y a veces hasta que se duerma. Hablar con calma o ayudar a su hijo a concentrarse en algo familiar puede ser reconfortante.

A medida que comienza la anestesia, su hijo puede:

- Poner los ojos en blanco hacia arriba
- Parecer inquieto y moverse
- Roncar o hacer ruidos extraños

Estas reacciones son normales y generalmente duran menos de un minuto. Aunque su hijo puede parecer despierto, no recordará esta parte de la experiencia.

## Recuperación después de la anestesia

Después del procedimiento, su hijo despertará en un área de recuperación donde será monitoreado de cerca. El tiempo de recuperación varía, pero muchos niños permanecen hasta tres horas.

Durante la recuperación, su hijo puede:

- Parecer confundido o inquieto o no reconocerle
- Sentir náuseas o vomitar
- Necesitar medicamentos para el dolor o contra las náuseas

Estos efectos son comunes y generalmente temporales. Un miembro del equipo de atención explicará qué esperar y cuándo su hijo estará listo para ir a casa.

## Recuperación y seguridad en casa

Después del procedimiento de su hijo, debe seguir las instrucciones del equipo de atención. Puede que necesite:

- Mantener a su hijo descansando y supervisado
- Ofrecer líquidos claros y evitar comidas pesadas
- Ayudar a su hijo a dormir de lado
- Limitar la actividad física por el resto del día

Para niños mayores y adolescentes, se debe evitar conducir, el alcohol, fumar y vapear después de la anestesia.

## Cuándo llamar para pedir ayuda

Llame al equipo de atención de su hijo si su hijo presenta:

- Un dolor de cabeza fuerte o dolor
- Náuseas o vómitos que duran más de cuatro horas
- Dificultad para beber líquidos o no ha orinado por 12 horas
- Somnolencia excesiva o inquietud

Llame al 9-1-1 o vaya a la sala de emergencias más cercana si su hijo:

- No puede despertarse del sueño
- Tiene la piel pálida, gris o azul
- Tiene respiración lenta o superficial

title.en: What to expect before your child gets anesthesia
title.es: Qué esperar antes de que su hijo reciba anestesia

markdown.en:
Your child's care team will provide instructions about eating, drinking, and medication use before anesthesia.

You will meet with a member of the pediatric anesthesia team before the procedure. This is a good time to:

- Ask questions and share any concerns
- Provide a complete medical history, including allergies, medications, and supplements
- Share your child's past experiences with anesthesia
- Let us know about a family history of anesthesia complications or neuromuscular conditions, such as muscular dystrophy
markdown.es:
El equipo de atención de su hijo proporcionará instrucciones sobre la alimentación, la bebida y el uso de medicamentos antes de la anestesia.

Se reunirá con un miembro del equipo de anestesia pediátrica antes del procedimiento. Este es un buen momento para:

- Hacer preguntas y compartir cualquier inquietud
- Proporcionar un historial médico completo, incluyendo alergias, medicamentos y suplementos
- Compartir las experiencias pasadas de su hijo con la anestesia
- Informarnos sobre antecedentes familiares de complicaciones con la anestesia o afecciones neuromusculares, como la distrofia muscular

markdown.en:
You may be able to stay with your child while they are prepared for anesthesia, and sometimes until they fall asleep. Talking calmly or helping your child focus on something familiar can be reassuring.

As anesthesia begins, your child may:

- Roll their eyes upward
- Seem restless and move around
- Snore or make funny noises

These reactions are normal and usually last less than a minute. Although your child may seem awake, they will not remember this part of the experience.

- Poner los ojos en blanco hacia arriba
- Parecer inquieto y moverse
- Roncar o hacer ruidos extraños

Estas reacciones son normales y generalmente duran menos de un minuto. Aunque su hijo puede parecer despierto, no recordará esta parte de la experiencia.

markdown.en:
After the procedure, your child will wake up in a recovery area where they are closely monitored. Recovery time varies, but many children stay for up to three hours.

During recovery, your child may:

- Seem confused or restless or not recognize you
- Feel nauseated or vomit
- Need pain or anti-nausea medication

These effects are common and usually temporary. A care team member will explain what to expect and when your child is ready to go home.
markdown.es:
Después del procedimiento, su hijo despertará en un área de recuperación donde será monitoreado de cerca. El tiempo de recuperación varía, pero muchos niños permanecen hasta tres horas.

Durante la recuperación, su hijo puede:

- Parecer confundido o inquieto o no reconocerle
- Sentir náuseas o vomitar
- Necesitar medicamentos para el dolor o contra las náuseas

Estos efectos son comunes y generalmente temporales. Un miembro del equipo de atención explicará qué esperar y cuándo su hijo estará listo para ir a casa.

markdown.en:
After your child's procedure, you should follow the care team's instructions. You may need to:

- Keep your child resting and supervised
- Offer clear liquids and avoid heavy meals
- Help your child sleep on their side
- Limit physical activity for the rest of the day

For older children and teens, driving, alcohol, smoking, and vaping should be avoided after anesthesia.
markdown.es:

- A bad headache or pain
- Nausea or vomiting that lasts more than four hours
- Trouble drinking fluids or has not urinated for 12 hours
- Excessive sleepiness or restlessness

- Can't wake up from sleep
- Has pale, gray, or blue skin
- Has slow or shallow breathing

title: Acute Bronchitis in Children

en.description: Bronchitis is an inflammation of the large breathing tubes (bronchi) in the lungs. Most cases are mild.

content.markdown:
## What is acute bronchitis in children?

Bronchitis is an inflammation of the large breathing tubes (bronchi) in the lungs. The illness can be short-term (acute) or long-term (chronic). Acute bronchitis means that the symptoms often develop quickly and don't last long. Most cases are mild.

## What causes acute bronchitis in a child?

Acute bronchitis is most often caused by a viral infection. It may also be caused by bacteria or things such as dust, allergens, strong fumes, or tobacco smoke.

The illness may develop after a cold or other viral infection in the nose, mouth, or throat (upper respiratory tract). Such illnesses can spread easily from direct contact with a person who is sick.

## What are the symptoms of acute bronchitis in a child?

The most common symptoms are:

- Dry or mucus-filled cough
- Vomiting or gagging
- Runny nose, often before a cough starts
- Chest congestion or pain
- An overall body discomfort or not feeling well
- Chills
- Slight fever
- Back and muscle pain
- Wheezing
- Sore throat

These symptoms often last 7 to 14 days. But the cough may continue for 3 to 4 weeks. These symptoms may look like other health problems. Make sure your child sees their doctor for a diagnosis.

## How is acute bronchitis diagnosed in a child?

Your child's doctor can often diagnose acute bronchitis with a health history and physical exam. In some cases, your child may need tests to rule out other health problems, such as pneumonia or asthma. These tests may include:

- **Chest X-rays.** This test makes images of internal tissues, bones, and organs.
- **Pulse oximetry.** An oximeter is a small device that measures the amount of oxygen in the blood. For this test, the doctor puts a small sensor (like a clip) on your child's finger or toe. When the device is on, a small red light can be seen in the sensor. The sensor is painless, and the red light does not get hot.
- **Sputum and nasal discharge samples.** These tests can find the germ causing an infection.

## How is acute bronchitis treated in a child?

Treatment will depend on your child's symptoms, age, and general health. It will also depend on how severe the condition is.

In nearly all cases, antibiotics shouldn't be used to treat acute bronchitis. That's because most of the infections are caused by viruses. Even children who have been coughing for longer than 8 to 10 days often don't need antibiotics. Antibiotics aren't used unless your child has a bacterial infection.

The goal of treatment is to help ease symptoms. Treatment may include:

- Plenty of rest
- Acetaminophen or ibuprofen (for children over 6 months) for fever and mild pain, if directed by your child's doctor
- Cough medicine for children over 4 years old, if directed by your child's doctor
- More fluids
- Cool-mist humidifier in your child's room

Talk with your child's doctor before giving over-the-counter cough and cold medicine to your child. The American Academy of Pediatrics does not advise giving these medicines to children younger than 4 years old because they may cause harmful side effects. For children between ages 4 and 6, only use over-the-counter products when advised by your child's doctor. In most cases, also don't give antihistamines. They can dry up the secretions. That can make the cough worse.

**Never give aspirin to a child or teen.** It could cause a rare but serious condition called Reye syndrome.

Most children who have acute bronchitis will get better without any problems. But the illness can lead to pneumonia.

## How can you help prevent acute bronchitis in your child?

You can help prevent acute bronchitis by stopping the spread of viruses that may lead to it. Take these steps:

- Teach your child to cover their nose and mouth when coughing or sneezing
- Make sure your child washes their hands often
- Keep your child up-to-date on all vaccines, including the yearly flu shot
- Keep your child away from others who are sick. If your child is sick, keep them away from others

## When should you contact your child's doctor?

Contact your child's doctor right away if your child's symptoms get worse, if new symptoms develop, or if your child:

- Has a high fever
- Can't keep liquids down
- Isn't eating or drinking
- Isn't having wet diapers

**Call 911 if your child:**

- Has trouble breathing
- Turns blue in color, especially the lips or fingertips
- Is breathing very fast

*This information is not intended as a substitute for professional medical care. Always follow your healthcare professional's instructions.*

title: Pediatric Pulmonary Medicine

en.description: The Pediatric Pulmonary Medicine Program has provided comprehensive care for children with respiratory disorders for more than 40 years.

content.markdown:
The Pediatric Pulmonary Medicine Program at Mass General Brigham for Children has provided comprehensive care for children with respiratory disorders for more than 40 years. The group provides multidisciplinary consultation, diagnostic and management services for a wide array of pulmonary conditions, including:

- Asthma
- Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
- Cystic fibrosis
- Recurrent and persistent pneumonias
- Unusual respiratory infections
- Aerodigestive disorders
- Immune deficiencies
- Congenital lung malformations
- Genetic pulmonary conditions
- Neuromuscular disorders leading to chronic lung problems
- Interstitial lung disease
- Apnea
- Exercise-related disorders
- Sleep-related breathing problems

We constantly strive to deliver the best family-centered, cutting-edge pediatric pulmonary care in close association with local primary care providers.

People with autism, and their loved ones, can benefit from specialized therapies and supportive services. At the Lurie Center for Autism, we customize care plans to help those with autism and other developmental disorders achieve their full potential.

en.description: Know-your-rights basics for non-citizens — finding a lawyer, ICE encounters, hospital protections, and sanctuary cities.

content.markdown:
> ⚠️ **This resource was last updated February 2017.** Immigration policy and enforcement practices have changed since then. Use this as a starting point, but consult an immigration lawyer or current legal-aid resource for up-to-date guidance.

If you do not have a current legal immigration status, we strongly encourage you to talk with an experienced immigration lawyer.

## Find an Immigration Lawyer

- **Boston-area FREE immigration clinics**
  - Boston Residents: the [Mayor's Office of New Bostonians](https://www.cityofboston.gov/newbostonians/programs/advice.asp) offers monthly free immigration clinics. See website for schedule.
  - [Irish International Immigrant Center (IIIC)](https://iiicenter.org/) — free immigration clinic for immigrants from any country.
- [Mass Legal Services — Find Legal Aid](http://www.masslegalservices.org/FindLegalAid)
- [Mass Immigrant and Refugee Advocacy Coalition (MIRA)](https://www.miracoalition.org/) — call **617-350-5480** and ask for their list of immigration lawyers.

## Know Your Rights

Make sure you and others know what to do if an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent stops you.

**You have a right to remain silent — whatever your immigration status.** You can refuse to speak to an ICE agent. Do not answer any questions, especially about your birth place, immigration status, or how you entered the United States.

There are **rights cards** that you can carry with you that say in English that you want to remain silent and that you want to speak with a lawyer. Carry a rights card with you. Download a card from:

content.label: National Immigration Law Center — Everyone Has Certain Basic Rights
ILRC Red Cards

content.markdown:
If ICE agents approach you on the street, ask if you are free to leave. If the agents say yes, calmly and silently walk away. If the agents say no, say you want to remain silent and to speak with a lawyer (or show them your rights card).

**You have the right to see a warrant** before letting anyone into your home. Slide your rights card under the door. Do not open the door unless an ICE agent shows you a warrant signed by a judge with the correct name and address of the person they are looking for on it. Ask them to slip the warrant under the door or show it to you through a window before you open the door.

**You have the right to speak with a lawyer and the right to make a phone call.** Make sure to carry the phone number for an immigration lawyer with you. You have the right to refuse to sign anything before you talk to a lawyer. You have the right to refuse to show any documents before you talk to a lawyer. **Never lie or give false information** to an immigration agent or police officer. Do not carry false identity cards or papers with you.

## Make a Safety Plan

These websites offer helpful tips:

- [ILRC Community Resources](https://www.ilrc.org/community-resources) and [Know Your Rights and What Immigrant Families Should Do Now](https://www.ilrc.org/know-your-rights-and-what-immigrant-families-should-do-now) — available in Spanish and Chinese
- [American Friends Service Committee — Know Your Rights](https://afsc.org/) — available in Spanish
- [Immigrant Defense Project](https://www.immigrantdefenseproject.org/know-your-rights-with-ice/)

## Your Rights in the Hospital

Most of the time ICE agents are supposed to avoid sensitive locations such as hospitals and doctors' offices — also schools, places of worship, weddings and funerals, and public demonstrations. ICE agents can enter these places if they get a supervisor's approval, or in situations related to national security, terrorism, or public safety, or where there is an imminent risk of destruction of evidence in an ongoing criminal case.

*The new President could change this policy to allow agents to enter sensitive locations more freely.*

For more information see: [DHS — Frequently Asked Questions on Existing Guidance for Enforcement Actions](https://www.dhs.gov/news/2016/07/15/fact-sheet-frequently-asked-questions-existing-guidance-enforcement-actions-or).

## Sanctuary Cities Offer Protection — But Not As Much as You May Think

Sanctuary status is meant to build trust between immigrants and local police. Rules vary, but typically local police in sanctuary cities will not ask victims or witnesses about their immigration status, and will not hold immigrants charged with minor crimes for ICE after they would otherwise be released.

Don't be confused by the word *"sanctuary."* Immigration laws are still in force in these places. It's just that the federal government has to enforce the laws — not the local police.

Some colleges offer sanctuary to their undocumented students. If the federal government says *"give me the names of your non-citizens,"* the colleges can refuse. But if ICE returns with a warrant, the colleges will have to provide the information.

If ICE agents approach you on the street, ask if you are free to leave. If the agents say yes, calmly and silently walk away. If the agents say no, say you want to remain silent and to speak with a lawyer (or show them your rights card).

title: Healthy Sleep Habits for Your Baby

en.description: Build a consistent bedtime routine, follow safe-sleep guidelines, and help your baby learn to fall asleep on their own.

content.markdown:
It is hard to imagine, but you will get a full night of uninterrupted sleep again. This resource provides tips to help build healthy sleep habits for your baby so you will all get better sleep.

## Why is this important?

Most babies do not figure out how to be "good" sleepers on their own. It is a process that takes time, patience, and practice — just like many other things as our children grow. Illness can sometimes lead to setbacks where you need to adjust the sleep routine. Keep an open mind and remember that if you can build healthy sleep habits from the start, you are moving in the right direction.

## When should we start?

A baby's sleep pattern begins to change around 3–4 months old as they start to have sleep cycles more like adults. Babies can have trouble staying asleep between sleep cycles. This is a good time to work with your baby on self-soothing strategies, so when they wake up in the middle of the night, they have the skills to get back to sleep without your help.

## Sleep associations

Spend some time observing your baby's sleep patterns — including when they typically nap and when they sleep longer at night. Do they typically need to be held or rocked to fall asleep? Do they usually fall asleep while feeding?

If you answered "yes" to the questions above, your baby has developed a sleep association that involves needing **you** to fall asleep. Teaching new sleep associations that don't require you to step in will help.

## Routines and sleep environment

Try to create a calm and consistent bedtime routine around the same time every night. This will help signal to your baby that it is time to wind down.

If your baby always falls asleep on the bottle or breast, consider feeding them outside of the bedroom to try to remove the association of feeding and sleeping. If they typically fall asleep while feeding before even getting to the bedtime routine, consider moving the feeding time up a bit earlier.

When it is bedtime:

- Set a comfortable room temperature (**68–72°F**)
- Turn down the lights
- Minimize loud noises — consider a white noise machine if your house is noisy

Try some bedtime activities after the last feed — a warm bath, baby massage, reading a story, or singing the same song. Try to do things in the same order each night. Be sure all caretakers follow the same routine. **Consistency is key.**

## Safe sleep guidelines

Follow the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommendations for safe sleep to lower the risk of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS):

- Put your baby to sleep on their back on a firm mattress
- Avoid soft bedding or bumpers
- Share a room, but not the bed
- Stop swaddling and switch to a wearable sleep sack as soon as your baby shows signs of trying to roll over

## Awake but drowsy

Finding the right time to put your baby to sleep in the crib is very important. A key phrase you'll see repeated in sleep resources is **"awake but drowsy"** — putting your baby to bed when they are tired or ready to sleep but still awake.

Watch for cues during the bedtime routine that your baby is getting tired. You may notice a lowered activity level, less eye contact, or eye rubbing. This is the best time to put your baby in the bassinet or crib — before they get overtired and fussy.

If your baby cries when you put them in the crib, you might try singing a song or saying "I love you" and then walking out of the room. Use the same reassuring song or words night after night.

Crying is natural but can be hard to hear. Set a timer and wait a few minutes before checking in again. If you need to go back in, try not picking them up — you might pat them or sing the song again. With each night sticking to the same routine, your baby will learn to fall asleep on their own.

Remember: it is **much easier** to teach this to a 4–5 month-old than to an older baby or toddler.

## Wake windows and naps

**Sleep often begets sleep.** Timing naps and bedtime is key. Try to get a sense of your baby's *wake window* — the amount of time that your baby is awake before they start to get tired. This will vary by age and is typically **1.5–3 hours** for 2- to 4-month-olds. If you wait too long and miss the window, your baby will start to get overtired and will be harder to put to sleep.

Also, watch out for long, late afternoon naps. These may make it harder for your baby to be ready to sleep at bedtime.

A baby who learns to fall asleep at night on their own is more likely to fall back asleep on their own if they wake up, so work on "awake but drowsy" first.

## Night awakenings

It is normal for sleepers, even adults, to briefly wake up at night as they go through their sleep cycles. A baby that "sleeps through the night" is a baby that falls back to sleep quietly in the middle of the night without crying out for their caregiver.

If your baby wakes up at night, give them a few minutes to see if they can fall back to sleep on their own. If your baby can see you from the crib, consider installing a physical barrier like a curtain to remove the visual contact. If you go to your baby, keep the room dark and avoid talking and eye contact — so your baby doesn't think it is playtime. Be gentle and reassuring.

Remember that your baby won't learn to sleep better right away, and there is not one perfect method to teach them. The goal is to help your baby feel calm with less of your involvement over time. Talk to your baby's pediatrician if you need help.

## More resources

**Websites**

- [HealthyChildren.org](https://www.healthychildren.org) (AAP) — search *"Getting Your Baby to Sleep"* and *"Self-Soothing: Help Your Baby Learn This Life Skill"*
- [ZeroToThree.org](https://www.zerotothree.org) — search *"sleep"*
- [BabySleep.com — Advice by Child Age](https://www.babysleep.com/advice/by-child-age/)
- [Dr. Craig Canapari](https://drcraigcanapari.com)
- [Babywise Mom](https://www.babywisemom.com)

**Books**

- *The No-Cry Sleep Solution* — Elizabeth Pantley
- *The Happiest Baby Guide to Great Sleep* — Harvey Karp
- *Solve Your Child's Sleep Problems* — Richard Ferber
- *The Baby Sleep Solution* — Suzy Giordano
- *Healthy Sleep Habits, Happy Child* — Marc Weissbluth
- *The CALM Baby Method: Solutions for Fussy Days and Sleepless Nights* — Fishbein and Ideran
- *It's Never Too Late to Sleep Train* — Craig Canapari

en.description: Drowning is the leading cause of unintentional death in MA kids — swim skills, supervision, pool gates, and CPR.

content.markdown:
Going for a swim in the pool or lake is a great way to keep cool in the summer heat. While taking a dip in the water is a lot of fun, it's important to know how to prevent children from drowning. **Drowning is the leading cause of unintentional injury and death in children ages 0–14 in Massachusetts.** Here are some tips for preventing drowning when your children go for a swim.

## How can I prevent my younger child from drowning?

For babies, younger children, and people who have less experience swimming, it's important to have an adult nearby who knows how to swim and can watch for danger. Also follow these tips:

- **Make sure your child learns how to swim.** If your child knows how to swim, they will be safer and more confident in the water — whether it's a pool, lake, or other body of water.
- **Learn how to swim if you don't know how.** If you know how to swim, you can help teach your child how to swim and stay safe in the water. You can also help your child if they are ever in danger.
- **Never leave your child alone in the water — even for a moment.** You should always be an arm's length away from your child in the water, including a bathtub. Your child can drown in even a few inches of water if they are not watched carefully.
- **Learn CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation).** CPR is a lifesaving technique that can help your child or others who are near drowning. Many schools or community centers, like your local YMCA, offer classes to learn CPR.

> **Did you know?** When a child is drowning, it's often silent and happens very quickly. Children don't splash or yell for help when drowning, like you'd see on TV or in a movie. Children can go underwater quickly — especially in strong currents like the ocean. If you notice your child is missing, check the water first to see if they went underwater.

## How can I prevent my older child from drowning?

For older children, teenagers, and people with more experience swimming, it's still important to have an adult nearby who knows how to swim and can watch for danger. Also follow these tips:

- **Make sure your child learns how to swim.** If your child knows how to swim, they will be safer and more confident in the water.
- **Learn how to swim if you don't know how.** You can help teach your child to swim and stay safe in the water, and help them if they are ever in danger.
- **If your older child knows how to swim, have them swim with a buddy.** Swimming buddies are fun and allow each person to look out for the other in case of danger.
- **Put a gate with a lock around your pool.** This way, your child won't be able to get into the pool without an adult to watch them. Store the key in a safe place.
- **Talk to your child about avoiding alcohol while swimming.** This is especially important for teenagers. Alcohol plays a part in up to half of all teenage and adult drowning accidents in the United States. Make sure you and your children don't drink alcohol near or in any type of water.
- **Learn CPR.** CPR is a lifesaving technique that can help your child or others who are near drowning. Many schools or community centers, like your local YMCA, offer classes to learn CPR.

title: How to Keep Your Child Safe During Your PICU Stay

en.description: A checklist for parents and guardians — ID bracelets, hand hygiene, room safety, and how to spot the care team.

content.markdown:
During a hospital stay, your child's health and safety is the care team's priority. As a parent or guardian, you are also an important part of the care team. Below is a checklist of ways you can help keep your child safe during a hospital stay.

## Identification

Each new day you will receive a sticker from the Unit Coordinators at the front desk of the PICU. The sticker will have both your room number and date. The sticker must be worn at all times in plain view for all family and visitors on the PICU.

## Preventing the spread of germs

- **Before entering your child's room,** wash your hands with soap and water.
- **After using the restroom or changing diapers,** wash your hands with soap and water.

## On the unit

- **Before entering the unit, use the intercom.** A staff member can let you in.
- **Do not hold the doors open for anyone you do not know.**
- **If your child has guests visiting,** ask visitors to use the intercom and check in at the front desk. They should also wear a visitor sticker at all times.

## In the hospital room

- **To prevent falls and injury,** move slowly around your child's crib or bedside and wear non-skid slippers or shoes.
- **If your child feels weak or dizzy,** ask the care team for help before moving your child.
- **Keep the guardrails up on your child's crib or hospital bed,** even if you only turn away or leave the room for a moment.
- **Keep the hospital room free of clutter.** Bring only what you and your child need during the hospital stay. Keep personal items out of the way where people walk.

## The care team

- All staff have a picture ID. You can ask to see a care team member's ID badge at any time.

description.en: A checklist for parents and guardians — ID bracelets, hand hygiene, room safety, and how to spot the care team.

markdown.en: During a hospital stay, your child's health and safety is the care team's priority. As a parent or guardian, you are also an important part of the care team. Below is a checklist of ways you can help keep your child safe during a hospital stay.

Each new day you will receive a sticker from the Unit Coordinators at the front desk of the PICU. The sticker will have both your room number and date. The sticker must be worn at all times in plain view for all family and visitors on the PICU.

- **Before entering your child's room,** wash your hands with soap and water.
- **After using the restroom or changing diapers,** wash your hands with soap and water.

- **Before entering the unit, use the intercom.** A staff member can let you in.
- **Do not hold the doors open for anyone you do not know.**
- **If your child has guests visiting,** ask visitors to use the intercom and check in at the front desk. They should also wear a visitor sticker at all times.

- **To prevent falls and injury,** move slowly around your child's crib or bedside and wear non-skid slippers or shoes.
- **If your child feels weak or dizzy,** ask the care team for help before moving your child.
- **Keep the guardrails up on your child's crib or hospital bed,** even if you only turn away or leave the room for a moment.
- **Keep the hospital room free of clutter.** Bring only what you and your child need during the hospital stay. Keep personal items out of the way where people walk.
- All staff have a picture ID. You can ask to see a care team member's ID badge at any time.

title: What to Expect: Emergency Department

en.description: A child-friendly tour of the pediatric ED with Wendy — what to expect during an emergency room visit.

content.markdown:
Coming to the Emergency Department can feel scary for children. This short video — *You Are Here: Wendy's Welcome to the ED* — gives kids a tour of what to expect when they arrive: the people they'll meet, the rooms they'll see, and what happens at each step.

Watching it together before a visit (or revisiting after one) can help children feel more in control of an unfamiliar experience.

content.caption: You Are Here: Wendy's Welcome to the ED — Mass General Hospital

content.markdown:
## About the video

A trip to the Emergency Department is stressful for patients, particularly for children. *You Are Here: Wendy's Welcome to the ED* explains what pediatric patients can expect during an emergency room visit and gives children insight into their healthcare experience.

The nine-minute piece is narrated by Wendy and uses stop-motion animation. It provides step-by-step introductions about what to expect during trauma care and highlights the department's child-focused features, including interactive LED lights that help soothe patients and child life specialists.

Wendy Wooden and her mother, Darcy Daniels, are very familiar with Mass General Brigham for Children's Emergency Department and inpatient units. Wendy was diagnosed at age 3 with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), caused by an E. coli infection, and has a complex medical history including heart failure, kidney and pancreatic damage that required a kidney transplant, and a partial intestinal removal at age 5. Her care has spanned five pediatric subspecialties.

While Wendy is a frequent patient accustomed to beeping machines and procedures, she says she still gets overwhelmed by urgent trips and admissions to the hospital. In 2014 — when a neighbor called for advice about what to expect when her two children were going to be in the hospital — Wendy realized that other children, less experienced with medical treatment, may feel similar anxieties.

With the help of her mother, Wendy wrote *You Are Here: Wendy's Welcome to the ED*, a guide for what fellow pediatric patients can expect during an emergency room visit and how to help reduce anxiety and foster communication between their parents and providers.

> "We've learned a lot over the years from the compassionate care we've received from Wendy's team of doctors, nurses, and other staff members. We wanted to share those lessons so other patients and families can get the best care possible while cutting down on stress and worry."
>
> — *Darcy Daniels, Wendy's mother and member of the Family Advisory Council*

title: Pediatric Imaging

en.description: What to expect during your child's X-ray, CT scan or MRI, with three short videos on preparing for, going through and finishing an MRI.

content.markdown:
Our pediatric radiologists and imaging specialists use advanced technology to provide an accurate diagnosis and make expert recommendations for your child’s care. We keep your child safe and comfortable throughout testing and make sure we get clear, detailed images.

### Pediatric Imaging Program

- 📞 [617-724-9729](tel:+16177249729)
- 🌐 [massgeneralbrigham.org/en/services/pediatric-imaging](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/en/services/pediatric-imaging)

Imaging tests can be overwhelming for a child. Whenever possible, parents or caregivers may stay with their child during exams. We also have child life specialists who use age-appropriate language and support techniques.

## Imaging tests for children

### CT and X-ray

We perform CT scans and X-rays using pediatric-specific protocols that markedly minimize radiation exposure. Exams are tailored to your child's age and size and are completed as efficiently as possible to reduce stress and discomfort.

### MRI

MRI uses magnetic fields, not radiation, to create detailed images of organs and soft tissues. Our teams help children stay comfortable during longer exams and communicate with them throughout the scan.

### Digestive and urinary imaging

We offer advanced imaging studies to evaluate digestive and urinary conditions in children, including MRI-based and fluoroscopic exams. Each study is carefully planned to meet your child's needs.

## MRI videos

These videos provide information about a child's MRI experience, how to prepare your child for an exam and what happens after an MRI.

es.description: Qué esperar durante la radiografía, la tomografía o la resonancia magnética de su hijo, con tres videos cortos en inglés sobre la resonancia.

content.markdown:
Nuestros radiólogos pediátricos y especialistas en imágenes utilizan tecnología avanzada para proporcionar un diagnóstico preciso y hacer recomendaciones expertas para el cuidado de su hijo. Mantenemos a su hijo seguro y cómodo durante las pruebas y nos aseguramos de obtener imágenes claras y detalladas.

### Programa Pediátrico de Diagnóstico por Imágenes

- 📞 [617-724-9729](tel:+16177249729)
- 🌐 [massgeneralbrigham.org/es/services/pediatric-imaging](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/es/services/pediatric-imaging)

Las pruebas de imágenes pueden ser abrumadoras para un niño. Siempre que sea posible, los padres o cuidadores pueden acompañar al niño durante los exámenes. También contamos con especialistas en vida infantil que utilizan un lenguaje apropiado para la edad y técnicas de apoyo.

## Pruebas de imágenes para niños

### CT y radiografías

Realizamos tomografías computarizadas y rayos X utilizando protocolos específicos para pediatría que reducen notablemente la exposición a la radiación. Los exámenes se adaptan a la edad y tamaño de su hijo y se completan de la manera más eficiente posible para reducir el estrés y la incomodidad.

### Resonancia magnética

La resonancia magnética utiliza campos magnéticos, no radiación, para crear imágenes detalladas de órganos y tejidos blandos. Nuestros equipos ayudan a los niños a mantenerse cómodos durante exámenes más largos y se comunican con ellos durante todo el escaneo.

### Imágenes digestivas y urinarias

Ofrecemos estudios de imágenes avanzados para evaluar condiciones digestivas y urinarias en niños, incluidos exámenes basados en resonancia magnética y fluoroscopia. Cada estudio se planifica cuidadosamente para satisfacer las necesidades de su hijo.

## Videos sobre la resonancia magnética

Estos videos, en inglés, explican la experiencia de un niño durante una resonancia magnética, cómo preparar a su hijo para el examen y qué pasa después.

en.description: How to prepare and support your child during IV placement and bloodwork — by age, with scripts and comfort techniques.

content.markdown:
At Mass General Hospital for Children, we are committed to making your child's IV or blood test as comfortable as possible. Your role is very important — children find it comforting when their parents are involved. This guide will give you some ideas about how you can best help your child.

## What should I tell my child?

Tell your child what is going to happen, and encourage your child to ask questions. You know your child best, and you know how much information your child can take in at a time.

## What can I do for my infant during the procedure?

It is very important to support your infant during the actual procedure. We recommend you:

- **Hold your baby** when possible. Soothing touch, such as rubbing your infant's head or back, also helps.
- **Swaddle your infant snugly** in a blanket so their entire body is covered. This helps your infant feel a sense of control.
- **Breastfeed your infant.** It is a familiar source of comfort and helps to distract your baby.
- **Give specially prepared sucrose (Sweet Ease).** Ask the staff if you are interested in this.
- **Distract your infant.** Talk and smile with younger infants, and play with older infants.

## How to answer your child's questions about the test or procedure

**Why do I need this done?**

The blood test will give the doctor information to help take care of you. Having an IV placed helps to give you important liquid or medicine that you can't swallow.

**What will happen to me?**

- They will clean the area where you need the blood test or IV. This will feel cool and may have a funny smell.
- A big rubber band called a tourniquet will be wrapped around your arm, giving your arm a tight hug.

**What should I do during the test?**

Your job is to hold still. It is OK to cry, but holding still will make the test go more quickly.

- They will tap on your arm to find veins. Veins are the small blue lines under your skin — the roads our blood uses to travel through the body.
- An IV is like a small straw that goes in your vein. The needle helps get the straw in, and will come out when the straw is in the vein.

> Be honest about the needle, but let your child know the needle will not be in for too long.

## What can I do for my child during the procedure?

**Distraction.** Distraction is the best way to calm your child. Pick something that will hold your child's attention — music, reading, blowing bubbles, talking (not about the hospital), or counting.

**Imagery.** Have your child think about a happy time. Talk about a memory, like a fun vacation, going down a roller coaster, or hitting a home run. You can help them get into the details — what were the sounds and smells around them, who else was there, and what it would be like if they did it again.

**Holding.** Many children like their parents to hold them during the procedure. If your child is young, they may want to sit on your lap. An older child may prefer you to hold their hand or rub their back.

## What can I do if I will not be with my child during a procedure?

Some parents prefer not to be with their child during a needle stick. There are also times when a child is hospitalized and parents are unable to make arrangements to be with their child. The staff will work with you to plan the best ways to help your child when you are not able to be there.

## Numbing medicine

There are local anesthetics or "numbing" medicines, which may make the *poke* hurt less. Some work quickly; others take a half hour to an hour to work. Many children like to use numbing medicine, but some children do not want to wait. Talk with your provider about the use of local anesthetics for your child. Make sure your child knows that they will feel some pressure during the procedure, even with the medicine.

## Praise and rewards

Praising your child right after the procedure is very important. If your child feels good about how it went, they are more likely to do well with other medical tests they may have. Let your child know they did well. Rewards like stickers or a special treat let your child know they have done a good job.

## Working with a child life specialist

A child life specialist is trained in preparing and supporting children and parents through medical tests. They can answer any questions that you have about how to best help your child. Tell your child's doctor or nurse if you would like to meet with a child life specialist.

## Let us know…

It is very helpful for us to know about your child's past experiences with blood tests and IV insertions. If these procedures have gone well in the past, let us know what worked. If your child has had difficulty tolerating these procedures, we will work with you and your child to improve the experience. Let us know if there have been any problems finding your child's veins in the past. Child life specialists are especially helpful for children who need additional preparation, help, and support.

title: Welcome to the PICU

en.description: Mass General for Children's 14-bed Pediatric Intensive Care Unit — services, care team, and contact information.

content.markdown:
## Contact Information

**Critical Care Medicine / PICU**
Bigelow Building, 55 Fruit Street, 6th Floor
Boston, MA 02114

- **Phone:** [617-724-4350](tel:+16177244350)
- **Fax:** 617-724-4391
- **Critical Transport (Pediatric Access Line):** [1-877-644-8988](tel:+18776448988) — connects directly to a critical care physician
- **Appointments:** [888-644-3248](tel:+18886443248)

## Overview

The Mass General for Children Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) is a **14-bed, multidisciplinary unit** that has distinguished itself by providing high-quality care for critically ill infants, children, and adolescents. Our patients present with a wide variety of life-threatening issues, such as severe infections, respiratory diseases, trauma, and post-operative care of various complex surgeries.

Our mission is to provide state-of-the-art critical care medicine by bringing together the most sophisticated technology and scientific advancement in an environment sensitive to the multicultural patients and families we serve. Excellent communication with the family and primary care pediatrician is seen as a critical success factor in optimizing outcomes.

content.caption: Welcome to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit — Mass General Brigham for Children

content.markdown:
## A coordinated multidisciplinary approach

The Mass General Brigham for Children PICU provides monitoring and life-sustaining treatment for critically ill patients suffering from a wide range of illnesses. We provide advanced cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological support — both invasive and non-invasive — including **extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO)**.

The PICU attendings are all trained in pediatric critical care medicine. In order to optimize the care of both the child and family, the pediatric intensivists, in collaboration with the critical care nurses, orchestrate a multidisciplinary team that includes medical and surgical physicians, as well as:

- Respiratory therapists
- Pediatric pharmacists
- Physical therapists
- Occupational therapists
- Child life specialists
- Social workers
- Chaplains
- Nutritionists
- Imaging and laboratory personnel

We have a complete range of pediatric consultant services, including:

- Pulmonology
- Endocrinology
- Cardiology and cardiac surgery
- Gastroenterology
- Hematology / oncology
- Infectious diseases
- Neurology
- Nephrology
- Trauma surgery
- General surgery
- Orthopaedic surgery
- Neurosurgery
- Transplant surgery
- Pediatric urology

The PICU fellowship program provides graduate-level patient supervision 24 hours a day.

At Mass General for Children, we strive to provide an open and welcoming environment. We believe that no one knows a child as well as parents do, and therefore parents — along with primary care providers — become **partners in the child's care**. Parents have an active voice in all treatment plans.

## A program of constant improvement

Our procedures and formulary are continually assessed through tools such as the Collaborative Practice Meeting, where novel therapies are evaluated and PICU performance is monitored. Quality assurance is provided through case studies and other forums. Scheduled educational activities are held in the PICU and, by arrangement, in the community.

### Service for sedation and pain-free procedures

The procedural sedation program provides analgesia and/or sedation as appropriate for children in need of potentially painful or anxiety-provoking procedures. This service is provided in a specially decorated, child-friendly patient room within the PICU, which is less intimidating than the operating room. Common procedures include lumbar punctures, bone marrow biopsies, kidney biopsies, central venous catheter placement, and knee taps.

### The TeleHealth program

The Pediatric TeleHealth program provides live video conferencing between the PICU and select patient rooms in emergency departments at outlying community hospitals — including MassGeneral for Children at Salem Hospital, Newton-Wellesley Hospital, and Nantucket Cottage Hospital. Through this link, the PICU staff may provide on-demand medical advice and guidance to help assess, and if needed, stabilize critically ill infants and children and prepare them for transport to the PICU. This telemedicine technology also supports an international link between the Buen Samaritano Hospital in Aguadilla, Puerto Rico and the PICU.

## Research

The Division of Pediatric Critical Care Medicine is performing laboratory and clinical research, including:

- Mechanisms of inflammation, apoptosis, and neuroprotection in brain injury
- Predictors of severity and outcome in severe, acute, and chronic pulmonary diseases
- Applications of innovative technology in the PICU environment

- Trauma surgery
- General surgery
- Orthopaedic surgery
- Neurosurgery
- Transplant surgery
- Pediatric urology

The PICU fellowship program provides graduate-level patient supervision 24 hours a day.

At Mass General for Children, we strive to provide an open and welcoming environment. We believe that no one knows a child as well as parents do, and therefore parents — along with primary care providers — become **partners in the child's care**. Parents have an active voice in all treatment plans.

Our procedures and formulary are continually assessed through tools such as the Collaborative Practice Meeting, where novel therapies are evaluated and PICU performance is monitored. Quality assurance is provided through case studies and other forums. Scheduled educational activities are held in the PICU and, by arrangement, in the community.

### Service for sedation and pain-free procedures

The procedural sedation program provides analgesia and/or sedation as appropriate for children in need of potentially painful or anxiety-provoking procedures. This service is provided in a specially decorated, child-friendly patient room within the PICU, which is less intimidating than the operating room. Common procedures include lumbar punctures, bone marrow biopsies, kidney biopsies, central venous catheter placement, and knee taps.

### The TeleHealth program

The Pediatric TeleHealth program provides live video conferencing between the PICU and select patient rooms in emergency departments at outlying community hospitals — including MassGeneral for Children at Salem Hospital, Newton-Wellesley Hospital, and Nantucket Cottage Hospital. Through this link, the PICU staff may provide on-demand medical advice and guidance to help assess, and if needed, stabilize critically ill infants and children and prepare them for transport to the PICU. This telemedicine technology also supports an international link between the Buen Samaritano Hospital in Aguadilla, Puerto Rico and the PICU.

The Division of Pediatric Critical Care Medicine is performing laboratory and clinical research, including:

- Mechanisms of inflammation, apoptosis, and neuroprotection in brain injury
- Predictors of severity and outcome in severe, acute, and chronic pulmonary diseases
- Applications of innovative technology in the PICU environment

title: Pediatric Emergency Department

en.description: Pediatric Emergency is a distinct child- and family-friendly service within general Emergency at Massachusetts General Hospital.

content.markdown:
Pediatric Emergency Medicine at Mass General Brigham for Children is child- and family-friendly and meets the highest standards of care.

The Pediatric Emergency Department cares for over 20,000 patients a year. Doctors and nurses specially trained in emergency medicine are available 24 hours a day to handle emergencies including serious illnesses and injuries. Infants, children, and adolescents are treated in a child-friendly setting, with a separate waiting room and exam rooms.

### Pediatric Emergency Department

- 55 Fruit Street, Boston, MA 02114
- 📞 [617-724-4110](tel:+16177244110)
- 🌐 [massgeneralbrigham.org/en/services/pediatric-emergency-medicine](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/en/services/pediatric-emergency-medicine)

Open 24 hours, every day

## Child- and family-friendly features

The pediatric ED has many child- and family-friendly features to help make your child's visit smooth and minimize stress for you and your child.

- Ten child-friendly, private rooms, including two rooms specifically for infectious disease
- Exam rooms that accommodate your child and family members if both need emergency care at the same time
- Child Life Specialists who help your child and family throughout the hospital experience through playtime, age-appropriate education about your child's care and preparing your child for procedures or exams
- A separate waiting area with pediatric-appropriate programming
- Televisions and DVD controls in every room
- Relaxing interactive LED lights above every bed

## Full range of services

- On-site radiology with low doses of radiation, adjusted appropriately for your child's age
- On-site fluoroscopy with low doses of radiation, adjusted appropriately for your child's age
- 24-hour psychiatric coverage
- The option for sedation to facilitate painful procedures is always available when clinically appropriate
- Access to all of the world-class resources at Massachusetts General Hospital, and Mass General Brigham for Children, including pediatric surgery and intensive care units

Our Mass General Brigham for Children pediatric trauma centers are verified by the American College of Surgeons as a Level I (highest level) pediatric trauma center, capable of providing state-of-the-art emergency care to the most critically injured children.

## Our triage system

When you arrive, a triage nurse reviews your child's symptoms, medical history, and vital signs. The triage nurse then determines when your child can be seen by one of our doctors trained in pediatric emergency medicine. Depending on the nature of a child's condition or symptoms, they might not always be seen in the order of their arrival:

- **If your child has a life-threatening condition,** they will be evaluated right away.
- **If your child's condition is not life-threatening,** they will be evaluated as soon as possible.

es.description: El Departamento de Emergencias Pediátricas atiende a más de 20,000 pacientes al año.

content.markdown:
La Medicina de Emergencia Pediátrica en Mass General Brigham para Niños es amigable para niños y familias y cumple con los más altos estándares de atención.

El Departamento de Emergencias Pediátricas atiende a más de 20,000 pacientes al año. Médicos y personal de enfermería con capacitación especializada en medicina de emergencias están disponibles las 24 horas del día para atender emergencias, incluidas enfermedades y lesiones graves. Los bebés, niños y adolescentes reciben atención en un entorno adaptado para ellos, con una sala de espera y consultorios separados.

### Departamento de Emergencias Pediátricas

- 55 Fruit Street, Boston, MA 02114
- 📞 [617-724-4110](tel:+16177244110)
- 🌐 [massgeneralbrigham.org/es/services/pediatric-emergency-medicine](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/es/services/pediatric-emergency-medicine)

Abierto las 24 horas, todos los días

## Características amigables para niños y familias

El Departamento de Emergencia Pediátrica tiene muchas características amigables para niños y familias para ayudar a que la visita de su hijo sea fluida y minimizar el estrés tanto para usted como para su hijo.

- Diez habitaciones privadas adaptadas para niños, incluyendo dos habitaciones específicamente para enfermedades infecciosas
- Salas de examen que acomodan a su hijo y a los miembros de la familia si ambos necesitan atención de emergencia al mismo tiempo
- Especialistas en Vida Infantil que ayudan a su hijo y a su familia durante toda la experiencia hospitalaria a través del juego, educación apropiada para la edad sobre el cuidado de su hijo y la preparación de su hijo para procedimientos o exámenes
- Un área de espera separada con programación adecuada para niños
- Televisores y controles de DVD en cada habitación
- Luces LED interactivas relajantes sobre cada cama

## Gama completa de servicios

- Radiología en el lugar con dosis bajas de radiación, ajustadas adecuadamente a la edad de su hijo
- Fluoroscopia en el lugar con dosis bajas de radiación, ajustadas adecuadamente a la edad de su hijo
- Cobertura psiquiátrica las 24 horas
- La opción de sedación para facilitar procedimientos dolorosos siempre está disponible cuando es clínicamente apropiado
- Acceso a todos los recursos de clase mundial del Massachusetts General Hospital y Mass General Brigham for Children, incluyendo cirugía pediátrica y unidades de cuidados intensivos

Nuestros centros de trauma pediátrico de Mass General Brigham para Niños están verificados por el Colegio Americano de Cirujanos como un centro de trauma pediátrico de Nivel I (el más alto), capaz de proporcionar atención de emergencia de última generación a los niños más críticamente heridos.

## Nuestro sistema de triaje

Cuando llegue, una enfermera de triaje revisará los síntomas, el historial médico y los signos vitales de su hijo. La enfermera de triaje decidirá entonces cuándo puede atender a su hijo uno de nuestros médicos especializados en medicina de emergencia pediátrica. Según la naturaleza de la afección o los síntomas, es posible que los niños no siempre sean atendidos en el orden en que llegaron:

- **Si su hijo tiene una afección que pone en peligro su vida,** será evaluado de inmediato.
- **Si la afección de su hijo no pone en peligro su vida,** será evaluado lo antes posible.

title: PICU Welcome Guide

en.description: Tips for your stay in the PICU — visiting hours, medical rounds, the family lounge, sleep rooms, food, parking, and more.

content.markdown:
We would like to partner with you to ensure a safe and comfortable healing environment for all our children and families. Here are some tips for your stay in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit.

At Mass General Brigham for Children, we strive to provide an open and welcoming environment. We believe that no one knows a child as well as parents do, and therefore parents, along with primary care providers, become partners in the child’s care. The parents have an active voice in all treatment plans.

### Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU)

Bigelow Building, 6th floor

- 55 Fruit Street, Boston, MA 02114
- 📞 [617-724-4350](tel:+16177244350)
- 🌐 [Learn more about the PICU](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/en/services/pediatric-critical-care-medicine)

content.caption: Welcome to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit — Mass General Brigham for Children

content.markdown:
## Visiting

- **Visiting hours:** 8:00 am – 8:00 pm
- For the safety and comfort of all our patients, we are able to accommodate **one parent or guardian per patient overnight**
- Please limit the number of visitors at the bedside to **2 people**
- Siblings are welcome to visit. For the safety of all our patients, siblings may not be left unattended and may not stay overnight.
- Visitors (including siblings) who are sick are asked to please stay home until their symptoms resolve.

## Medical Rounds

Each morning the PICU team will gather outside of your child's room to review information and make a plan of care for the day. **You are invited to participate in rounds.**

After rounding on all of the patients, your doctors will be available to review your child's care plan and answer questions.

## Family Lounge

You are welcome to use the Family Lounge, located around the corner from the Bigelow elevators outside the PICU. It includes:

- A sink, refrigerator, microwave, and coffee
- A table and chairs where you can eat and relax
- A community bathroom with a shower that is wheelchair accessible

Please ask your child's nurse for a towel if needed.

## Where can I sleep?

Sleep rooms are available on a nightly basis. These rooms are given out based on availability and patient condition.

- If you are given a sleep room, please remove your belongings **by 10 am the next day**
- If you need a sleep room for another night, please speak with the Unit Coordinator at the front desk

## Where can I wash my clothes?

There is a washer and dryer located on the inpatient pediatric floor, **Ellison 17**. Turn right when you leave the PICU, follow the signs to the Ellison elevators, and take them to floor 17. Laundry detergent can be provided upon request.

## What food is available?

MGH offers a wide variety of food to purchase in the cafeteria. Take the Bigelow elevators down to the basement (level "B") and follow the signs to **Eat Street Café**, in the Ellison Building's lower level.

You may also order a tray of food to be brought to your child's room, but there is a cost associated. If you have financial concerns, please talk to your child's nurse to request social work.

## What activities can my child have?

You are always welcome to bring any comfort items or toys from home. We also have toys, comfort items, and art supplies that can be provided to your child by our staff to help them during their stay. Request the **child life specialist** for more information.

## How can I validate parking?

To receive discounted parking, present your **PICU visitor sticker** to the attendant in the parking garage or in the Yawkey main lobby. Questions related to parking can be directed to the information desk or to your child's nurse.

---

*For more information, please speak with your child's nurse or the Unit Coordinator at the front desk.*

zh-Hant.description: 兒童加護病房入住提示 — 探視時間、醫療查房、家庭休息室、臥室、餐飲、停車等。

content.markdown:
我們願意與您合作,確保為我們所有的兒童和家庭提供安全舒適的治療環境。以下是您在兒童加護病房 (PICU) 入住時的一些提示。

### Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU)

Bigelow Building, 6th floor

- 55 Fruit Street, Boston, MA 02114
- 📞 [617-724-4350](tel:+16177244350)
- 🌐 [Learn more about the PICU](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/en/services/pediatric-critical-care-medicine)

content.caption: Welcome to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit — Mass General Brigham for Children

content.markdown:
## 訪客

- **探視時間:** 上午 11:00 – 晚上 8:00
- 為了所有患者的安全與舒適,我們能夠為每位患者安排**一位家長或監護人過夜**
- 請將床邊的訪客數量限制在 **2 人**
- 歡迎兄弟姊妹來訪。為了所有患者的安全,兄弟姊妹不得無人看管,也不得過夜
- 生病的訪客(包括兄弟姊妹)需要待在家裡,直到症狀消失為止

## 醫療查房

每天早上,PICU 團隊都會聚集在孩子的病房外,審查資訊並制定當天的照護計畫。**我們邀請您參加查房。**

在對所有患者查完房之後,您的醫生將可審查您孩子的照護計畫並回答問題。

## 家庭休息室

歡迎您使用位於 PICU 外 Bigelow 電梯附近的家庭休息室。這裡設有:

- 水槽、冰箱、微波爐與咖啡
- 桌子和椅子,您可以在那裡就餐和放鬆
- 帶淋浴間的公共盥洗室,輪椅可以使用

如果需要,請向孩子的護士要一條毛巾。

## 我在哪裡睡覺?

每晚都提供臥室。這些房間是根據可用性與患者情況分配的。

- 如果您分到臥室,請於**第二天早上 10 點之前**搬走您的物品
- 如果您需要再一個晚上的臥室,請諮詢前台的房間協調員

## 我在哪裡洗衣服?

**Ellison 17** 住院兒科樓層設有洗衣機和烘乾機。離開 PICU 後向右轉,按照指示牌到達 Ellison 電梯並前往 17 樓。洗衣清潔劑可應要求提供。

## 我可獲取什麼食物?

MGH 提供各種各樣的食物,可在自助餐廳購買。乘坐 Bigelow 電梯到地下層 (「B」層),然後按照指示牌前往 **Eat Street Café**。

您也可以在孩子的房間點一盤食物送到病房,但這是需要付費的。如果您有財務問題,請諮詢您的護士以請求社會工作。

## 我的孩子可以參加什麼活動?

歡迎您從家中帶來任何舒適的物品或玩具。我們也有玩具、舒適物品以及美術用品,可由我們的工作人員為您的孩子提供,以在他們住院期間帶來幫助。向**兒童生活專家**諮詢更多資訊。

## 如何驗證停車?

若要獲得折扣停車,請在停車場或 Yawkey 主大廳向管理員出示 **PICU 訪客貼紙**。有關停車的問題可以直接諮詢詢問台或您孩子的護士。

---

*如需瞭解更多資訊,請諮詢您孩子的護士或前台的房間協調員。*

es.description: Consejos para su estadía en la PICU — horario de visitas, visita del equipo médico, sala familiar, habitaciones para dormir, comida y estacionamiento.

content.markdown:
Quisiéramos colaborar con usted para garantizar un entorno de recuperación seguro y cómodo para todos nuestros niños y familias. Aquí tiene algunos consejos para su estadía en la Unidad de Cuidados Intensivos Pediátricos (PICU, por sus siglas en inglés).

En Mass General Brigham para Niños, nos esforzamos por proporcionar un ambiente abierto y acogedor. Creemos que nadie conoce a un niño tan bien como sus padres; por eso, los padres, junto con los proveedores de atención primaria, se convierten en colaboradores de la atención del niño. Los padres tienen una voz activa en todos los planes de tratamiento.

### Unidad de Cuidados Intensivos Pediátricos (PICU)

Edificio Bigelow, 6.º piso

- 55 Fruit Street, Boston, MA 02114
- 📞 [617-724-4350](tel:+16177244350)
- 🌐 [Más información sobre la PICU](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/es/services/pediatric-critical-care-medicine)

content.caption: Bienvenidos a la Unidad de Cuidados Intensivos Pediátricos — Mass General Brigham for Children

content.markdown:
## Visitantes

- **Horario de visitas:** 11:00 am – 8:00 pm
- Por la seguridad y comodidad de todos nuestros pacientes, solo podemos hospedar a **un padre, madre o tutor por paciente durante la noche**
- Por favor, mantenga un límite de **2 visitantes** en la habitación
- Le invitamos a los hermanos a hacer visitas. Por la seguridad de todos nuestros pacientes, los hermanos no pueden pasar la noche ni estar sin supervisión en la unidad.
- Le pedimos encarecidamente a todo visitante que esté enfermo — incluidos los hermanos — que permanezca en casa hasta que se hayan resuelto sus síntomas.

## Visita del equipo médico

Cada mañana, el equipo de la PICU se reunirá fuera de la habitación de su hijo para revisar su información y hacer un plan de atención para el día. **Le invitamos a participar en estas visitas.**

Después de hacerles la visita a todos los pacientes, los médicos de su hijo estarán disponibles para revisar con usted el plan de atención y responder sus preguntas.

## Sala familiar

Le invitamos a usar la sala familiar, ubicada fuera de la PICU al lado de los ascensores de Bigelow. La sala cuenta con:

- Lavamanos, refrigerador, microondas y café
- Una mesa y sillas donde puede comer y relajarse
- Un baño compartido con ducha accesible para sillas de ruedas

Puede pedirle una toalla a la enfermera de su hijo si la necesita.

## ¿Dónde puedo dormir?

Las habitaciones para dormir están disponibles en la noche. El uso de estas habitaciones está sujeto a disponibilidad y a la condición del paciente.

- Si se le proporciona una habitación, por favor retire sus pertenencias **a más tardar a las 10 am del día siguiente**
- Si necesita la habitación para alguna otra noche, por favor hable con el coordinador de la unidad

## ¿Dónde puedo lavar mi ropa?

Hay una lavadora y secadora en el **piso 17 del edificio Ellison**, en la unidad pediátrica de pacientes internados. Al salir de la PICU, gire a la derecha y siga las señales hasta los ascensores de Ellison; suba al piso 17. El detergente está disponible a pedido.

## ¿Hay opciones de comida?

Se vende una amplia variedad de comida en la cafetería del MGH. Tome los ascensores de Bigelow hasta el sótano (oprima "B" en el ascensor) y siga las señales hasta la cafetería **Eat Street Café**.

Puede pedir una bandeja de comida a la habitación de su hijo, pero esto tiene un costo asociado. Si está pasando por dificultades financieras, por favor pídale a la enfermera de su hijo que le ponga en contacto con un trabajador social.

## ¿Qué actividades puede hacer mi hijo?

Usted siempre puede traer de su casa algún juguete u objeto reconfortante o de valor sentimental. Nosotros también tenemos juguetes, objetos reconfortantes y materiales de arte que le podemos proporcionar a su hijo durante su estadía. Para obtener más información, pida una consulta con nuestro **especialista en vida infantil**.

## ¿Cómo obtengo la tarifa de descuento para el estacionamiento?

Para recibir la tarifa de descuento, presente su **vale de visitante de la PICU** al cajero en la planta baja del estacionamiento (garaje) o en el vestíbulo principal del Centro Yawkey. Puede dirigir cualquier pregunta acerca del estacionamiento a la enfermera de su hijo o al personal encargado de los mostradores de información.

---

content.caption: Welcome to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit — Mass General Brigham for Children

content.markdown:
## Vizitè

- **Orè vizit:** 11:00 am – 8:00 pm
- Pou sekirite ak konfò tout pasyan nou yo, nou kapab akeyi **yon (1) paran oswa responsab legal pou chak pasyan pandan nuit lan**
- Tanpri, limite kantite vizitè nan chanm pasyan an pou **2 moun**
- Nou ap kontan akeyi frè ak sè yo. Pou sekirite tout pasyan nou yo, nou pa kapab kite frè ak sè yo san siveyans, epi yo pa kapab pase nuit lan nan lopital la.
- Nou ap mande vizitè (san wete frè ak sè) ki malad yo pou rete lakay yo jiskaske sentòm yo a disparèt.

## Vizit medikal

Chak maten, ekip PICU a ap reyini deyò chanm timoun ou an pou revize enfòmasyon yo epi pou etabli yon plan swen pou jounen an. **Nou envite w patisipe nan vizit yo.**

Apre yo fin vizite tout pasyan yo, doktè ou yo ap disponib pou egzamine plan swen timoun ou an epi pou reponn kesyon ou yo.

## Salon familyal

Ou kapab itilize Salon Familyal la ki twouve li nan ang asansè Bigelow yo, deyò PICU a. Li gen:

- Yon evye, yon frijidè, yon mikwo-ond, ak kafe
- Yon tab ak chèz kote ou kapab manje epi detann ou
- Yon saldeben kominotè ki gen douch ki aksesib pou chèz woulant

Tanpri, mande enfimyè timoun ou an yon sèvyèt si sa nesesè.

## Ki kote mwen kapab dòmi?

Gen chanm pou dòmi ki disponib sou baz chak nuit. Nou atribye chanm sa yo selon disponibilite ansanm ak eta sante pasyan an.

- Si ou jwenn yon chanm pou dòmi, tanpri retire bagay pèsonèl ou yo **anvan 10 am nan demen**
- Si ou bezwen yon chanm pou pase yon lòt nuit, tanpri pale sou sa ak Kowòdonatè Inite a ki nan resepsyon an

## Ki kote mwen kapab lave rad mwen?

Gen yon machin a lave ak yon machin pou seche rad nan etaj pasyan ki entène yo, **Ellison 17**. Vire adwat lè ou kite PICU a, suiv pano ki endike asansè Ellison yo, epi monte nan etaj 17 la. Nou kapab bay pwodui netwayaj si ou mande sa.

## Ki manje ki disponib pou mwen?

MGH pwopoze yon pakèt varyete aliman pou achte nan kafeterya a. Pran asansè Bigelow yo rive jis nan etaj anba nèt la ("B"), epi suiv pano ki ekri **Eat Street Café** yo.

Ou kapab kòmande yon plato aliman nan chanm timoun ou an, men gen yon pri pou sa. Si ou gen pwoblèm finansyè, tanpri pale ak enfimyè ou a pou mande èd sosyal.

## Ki aktivite timoun mwen an kapab fè?

Ou kapab toujou vini ak nenpòt atik konfò oswa jwèt li gen lakay li. Epitou, nou gen jwèt, atik konfò, ak materyèl atizay manm pèsonèl nou an kapab bay timoun ou an pou ede li pandan tan li nan lopital la. Pou plis enfòmasyon, pale avèk **espesyalis lavi timoun nan**.

## Kijan mwen kapab valide pakin nan?

Pou w resevwa yon rediksyon sou pakin nan, montre **otokolan vizitè PICU ou a** bay moun ki nan pakin nan oswa ki nan chanm prensipal Yawkey a. Ou kapab poze kesyon ki gen rapò ak pakin yo nan biwo enfòmasyon an oswa bay enfimyè ou a.

---

*Pou plis enfòmasyon, tanpri pale avèk enfimyè timoun ou an oswa Kowòdonatè Inite a ki nan resepsyon an.*
