Mass General social workers are licensed mental health clinicians who provide **short-term individual, couple, family, and group therapy**.

## We can help you with

- Coping with illness, injury, treatment, and recovery
- Mental health or substance use concerns
- Grief and bereavement
- Relationships, parenting, or family concerns
- Abuse, neglect, violence, and other safety issues
- Job, school, or other life stresses

## Eligibility

If you get your primary medical care at Mass General and meet certain other criteria, you may qualify.

en.description: What mindfulness is, how it can help, three simple practices to try, and apps to support a daily habit — written for teens.

content.markdown:
Practicing mindfulness is a way to be present in your everyday life — whether you're at school, at home, or out with friends. Here you'll learn about mindfulness and how it can help you feel less stressed and live in the moment every day.

## What is mindfulness?

**Mindfulness** is being present and aware of the moment without judging your thoughts, feelings, and **body sensations** (what you feel physically). The past or future isn't on your mind. Instead, you are aware of how you feel and what you think here and now.

> **Did you know?** Mindfulness is not sitting still and doing nothing — but it can be if you want. Mindfulness is simply being aware of your thoughts, feelings, and surroundings, and not judging or getting wrapped up in them.

## How can mindfulness help me?

Mindfulness is helpful in many ways, including helping you:

- Do better in school
- Concentrate better in school and out of school
- Feel less stressed
- Sleep better at night
- Reduce pain in your body
- Cope with anxiety, depression, or other mental health issues
- Improve heart, stomach, and gut health

## How can I practice mindfulness?

The good thing about mindfulness is that you can do it **anywhere, any time**. You can even practice mindfulness around others and they would never know.

**Simply notice the sights, smells, and things that surround you.** Focus on what's there for you in the moment, right here, right now. If you find your mind starts to wander, that's okay. Find something in your surroundings to focus on that will bring you back to the here and now.

**Count your breaths, either aloud or in your head.** This is helpful if you're feeling stressed, nervous, or overwhelmed. Breathe in for 5 seconds, counting *1-2-3-4-5*. Breathe out for 5 seconds, counting *1-2-3-4-5*. Simply be aware of your stressed or nervous feelings. Don't judge those feelings or try to push them away — they will pass as you count and breathe.

**Release tension in your body.** Sit, stand, or lie down in a comfortable position. Simply notice where you feel tense or stressed. When you breathe in, picture yourself gathering the stress or worry into a cloud. When you breathe out, picture yourself releasing that stress or blowing the cloud away.

## Smartphone apps for mindfulness

There are many apps that can help you learn to practice and use mindfulness every day:

- **[Calm](https://www.calm.com)** — A meditation website and app designed to bring peace to your mind. Some content is free; longer programs are paid.
- **[MindShift CBT](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/mindshift-cbt-anxiety-relief/id634684825)** — A free app designed to teach you positive ways of coping with anxiety, stress, and feelings of being overwhelmed.

## A note for parents

Being mindful toward your teen, your friends and family, and your surroundings can help improve your own *and* your teen's mindfulness skills. Being mindful also includes being non-judgmental, kind, grateful, loving, patient, forgiving, trusting, open, generous, gentle, and curious.

---

*Revised August 2016. Created by Cate Medeiros, MGH Adolescent and Young Adult Medicine.*

en.description: How to model mindfulness for toddlers, two breathing exercises to practice together, and a quick S.T.O.P. technique for caregivers.

content.markdown:
Children and adults can benefit from practicing mindfulness — the process of pausing to bring attention to the present moment. Here you'll learn more about mindfulness, why it's important, and how you can start practicing mindfulness with your child on a regular basis.

## What is mindfulness?

**Mindfulness** is a way to purposefully pay more attention to our bodies, thoughts, and emotions. It helps your mind and body become more aware of the moment and create a feeling of inner calmness.

## Why is it important to teach mindfulness to young children?

Growing up can be very stressful starting from the moment you are born (picture a tired, hungry baby). Toddlers and preschoolers often struggle with self-control and language. Teaching mindfulness can give children and their caretakers a tool to decrease anxiety and improve patience for the rest of their lives.

The benefits of mindfulness include:

- Decreased stress and social anxiety
- Increased happiness, compassion (concern and caring for others), and empathy (the ability to understand and share the feelings of another)
- Improved attention, focus, and impulse control

## How do you practice mindfulness?

There are various ways to practice mindfulness: concentration, breathing exercises, thinking positively, and feeling and expressing gratitude.

### Start by practicing it yourself

- **Be fully present and engaged** when you are spending time with your child. Make eye contact. Don't look at your phone often when your child is around.
- **Treat other people kindly** even when you are feeling frustrated or upset.
- **Choose activities that involve focus, creativity, and curiosity** — such as reading or making art rather than watching TV.
- **Stay calm.** When your child gets upset, try not to become agitated.
- **Express gratitude** for what you are thankful for, and teach your child to do the same.

### Then try these tips with your toddler

- **Teach your child how to recognize their feelings** (both good and bad) and how to describe them through words or pictures.
- **Teach your child forgiveness.** If there is a problem, discuss it. Help your child understand the problem will get better. If a child misbehaves, make an effort to show that you forgive them.
- **Teach your child breathing exercises.** *(See below.)*

## What is mindful breathing?

As young children learn to manage strong emotions, deep breathing can be part of the process. Mindful breathing can help your child become more familiar with their body and its rhythms. You can practice it *in the moment* when your child is having trouble controlling their emotions (crying, frightened, screaming, hitting). You can also practice mindful breathing as part of your child's morning or bedtime routine. Practicing at times that are *not* stressful can make mindful breathing easier when tougher situations arise.

### Finger-Counting Breaths

A useful exercise to try anywhere to calm a child who is having a tantrum, or even just to take a moment to regroup. Do it together with your child.

1. Create gentle fists with your hands.
2. With each breath, take one finger out from your palm. For example, on your first exhale, open your right thumb from your fist. Pause and take a breath in.
3. On your next exhale, take out your right pointer finger. Pause and take a breath in.
4. Continue until all your fingers are uncurled.

### Deep Breaths Before Bed

Before bed, take a few minutes to calm your mind and body down with this exercise.

1. Take a deep breath in through the nose. As you breathe out, say *"three,"* but hold it out: *"threeee."*
2. Take another deep breath in. On the next breath out, say *"twoooo."*
3. Take a last deep breath in and let it out, saying *"one,"* but hold it out: *"onnee."*
4. Relax for a few more breaths and try to enjoy the feeling of calmness.
5. Repeat if desired.

## S.T.O.P. for parents and caregivers

This popular short exercise can be woven into your day anytime you are feeling stressed, upset, or out of touch with the present moment.

- **S — Stop.** Take a pause from what you are doing. Put things away for a minute.
- **T — Take a few deep breaths.** Feel the sensation of your own breathing. You can even say to yourself *"in"* and *"out"* as you inhale and exhale if it helps you concentrate.
- **O — Observe.** Take note of your thoughts, feelings, and emotions — good or bad. Name them and notice how they are affecting your body. What is your posture? Are you having aches or pains? Are you feeling worried?
- **P — Proceed.** If you can, do something that will support you in that moment (talk to a friend, have a cup of tea). Then continue what you were doing.

## Helpful resources for learning to practice mindfulness

- **[Mindfulness for Children](https://annakaharris.com/mindfulness-for-children/)** by Annaka Harris — audio instructions on mindful awareness exercises.
- **[Peace Out](http://bedtime.fm/peaceout)** — daily audio short stories that help children calm down and relax through visualization and breathing exercises.
- **A Handful of Quiet: Happiness in Four Pebbles** by Thich Nhat Hanh — guide written by a Zen monk for parents who would like to introduce mindfulness and meditation into their homes.
- **[Resources for Teaching Mindfulness to Your Children](https://leftbrainbuddha.com/resources-for-teaching-mindfulness-to-your-children/)** by Sarah Rudell Beach — lists popular resources (posts, books, websites) for learning mindfulness.
- **Have You Filled a Bucket Today?** by Carol McCloud — a book that encourages children to see how easy it is to express love, kindness, and appreciation.
- **Mindful Games** by Greenland and Harris — a card deck of 55 mindfulness exercises for kids.
- **Sitting Still Like a Frog** by Eline Snel — exercises for helping children with anxiety, improved concentration, and handling emotions.
- **Sitting Together** by Sumi Loundon Kim — a comprehensive guide to mindfulness for the entire family, including a guide for parents, lesson plans for children, and an activity book.

---

*Sources: Adapted from "Three Ways for Children to Try Meditation at Home," Jillian Pransky, New York Times (5/10/16); and "Stressing Out? S.T.O.P." from mindful.org, Elisha Goldstein, PhD (August 2013).*

*© MGHfC CARMA. Revised November 2018.*

en.description: Join a Patient and Family Advisory Council (PFAC) at Mass General Brigham to help improve patient care.

content.markdown:
Mass General Brigham's Patient and Family Advisory Councils (PFACs) bring together patients, family members, and hospital staff to improve the care experience. By sharing your insights, you can help shape hospital policies, programs, and services to enhance patient-centered care.

### Patient and Family Advisory Councils

- ✉️ [pfac@mgb.org](mailto:pfac@mgb.org)
- 🌐 [Apply online](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/en/forms/mgb-patient-and-family-advisory-application)
- 🌐 [massgeneralbrigham.org/en/patients-visitors/resources/patient-experience/patient-family-advisory-council](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/en/patients-visitors/resources/patient-experience/patient-family-advisory-council)

## What do PFACs do?

PFAC members help to improve the patient experience by:

- Providing feedback based on their personal experiences as patients or family members
- Collaborating with hospital staff and clinicians on committees
- Lending patient expertise in discussion groups, educational sessions, and other strategic initiatives
- Reviewing and helping to develop educational materials for patients and families
- Assisting in hospital planning efforts to improve patient care and services

## Who can be a patient and family advisor?

You may be eligible to become an advisor if you or a family member received care at a Mass General Brigham hospital in the past three years. No special qualifications are required — just a willingness to collaborate, provide feedback, and contribute to meaningful discussions.

## Which PFAC should I join?

Every Mass General Brigham hospital has at least one general PFAC, which are open to all patients and family members who have received care at that hospital in the past three years. Some larger hospitals also have specialty PFACs, which focus on specific topic areas.

Brigham and Women's Hospital and Massachusetts General Hospital also offer specialty PFACs focused on specific care areas, such as:

- Emergency Department (ED)
- Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU)

If you are interested in joining a specialty PFAC, contact us for more information.

content.label: Patient and Family Advisory Councils

content.markdown:
## How can I join a PFAC?

If you are interested in becoming a patient and family advisor, please fill out an application form. Once we receive your application, we'll reach out with the next steps.

Please note: You may only join one PFAC at a time, even if you are eligible for more than one. If you aren't sure which PFAC is the best fit for you, email us.

Al compartir sus perspectivas, puede ayudar a definir las políticas, los programas y los servicios del hospital para mejorar la atención centrada en el paciente.

### Consejos Asesores de Pacientes y Familias

- ✉️ [pfac@mgb.org](mailto:pfac@mgb.org)
- 🌐 [Presente su solicitud](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/es/forms/mgb-patient-and-family-advisory-application)
- 🌐 [massgeneralbrigham.org/es/patients-visitors/resources/patient-experience/patient-family-advisory-council](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/es/patients-visitors/resources/patient-experience/patient-family-advisory-council)

## ¿Qué hacen los PFAC?

Los integrantes de los PFAC ayudan a mejorar la experiencia del paciente de las siguientes maneras:

- Aportan comentarios basados en sus experiencias personales como pacientes o familiares
- Colaboran con el personal del hospital y los profesionales clínicos en comités
- Aportan su experiencia como pacientes en grupos de debate, sesiones educativas y otras iniciativas estratégicas
- Revisan y ayudan a desarrollar materiales educativos para pacientes y familias
- Colaboran en la planificación del hospital para mejorar la atención y los servicios para pacientes

## ¿Quién puede ser una persona asesora de pacientes y familias?

Puede reunir los requisitos para convertirse en una persona asesora si usted o un familiar recibió atención en un hospital de Mass General Brigham durante los últimos tres años. No se requieren cualificaciones especiales, solo disposición para colaborar, aportar comentarios y participar en conversaciones significativas.

## ¿A qué PFAC debo unirme?

Cada hospital de Mass General Brigham tiene al menos un PFAC general, abierto a todos los pacientes y familiares que hayan recibido atención en ese hospital durante los últimos tres años. Algunos hospitales más grandes también tienen PFAC especializados que se centran en temas específicos.

Brigham and Women's Hospital y Massachusetts General Hospital también ofrecen PFAC especializados centrados en áreas de atención específicas, como:

- Departamento de Emergencias (ED)
- Unidad de Cuidados Intensivos Neonatales (NICU)

Si desea unirse a un PFAC especializado, comuníquese con nosotros para obtener más información.

Tenga en cuenta: Solo puede participar en un PFAC a la vez, aunque reúna los requisitos para más de uno. Si no sabe qué PFAC es el más adecuado para usted, envíenos un correo electrónico.

en.description: Community organizations supporting families of children with serious illness, disabilities, or special health needs — across Massachusetts.

content.markdown:
A directory of community organizations and Massachusetts state services that support families caring for children with serious illness, disabilities, or special health needs.

## Courageous Parents Network (CPN)

The Pediatric Supportive & Palliative Care team collaborates closely with the Courageous Parents Network. CPN is a destination created by parents, for parents — to support, guide, and strengthen families as they care for a seriously ill child. You'll find wisdom from fellow parents and pediatric care providers to help you be the best parent you can be to your child and get through each moment. CPN has guides, videos, and podcasts available for families.

- ✉️ [Connect@courageousparentsnetwork.org](mailto:Connect@courageousparentsnetwork.org)
- 🌐 [courageousparentsnetwork.org](https://courageousparentsnetwork.org/)

## Department of Developmental Services (DDS)

The Massachusetts Department of Developmental Services offers services and supports for individuals with intellectual disabilities and children with developmental disabilities. DDS offers residential supports, services for families, respite care, and transportation services. Some services are provided directly by DDS, and others are available from providers in the community. **Applying early allows families to access supports as needed.**

Once a child turns 22 years old, DDS takes over day-to-day services from the child's school district — typically as day supports or a day program.

- 📞 [617-727-5608](tel:+16177275608)
- ✉️ [DDSInfo@mass.gov](mailto:DDSInfo@mass.gov)
- 🌐 [mass.gov/orgs/department-of-developmental-services](https://www.mass.gov/orgs/department-of-developmental-services)

## Family Ties of Massachusetts

Parents of children with special needs often struggle with their emotions around the everyday challenges they face. This may happen at the time of your child's diagnosis — and recur with a new diagnosis, as well as throughout the many transitions from infancy through adulthood.

- 📞 [800-905-8437](tel:+18009058437)
- 🌐 [massfamilyties.org](https://www.massfamilyties.org)

## Federation for Children with Special Needs

Provides information, support, and assistance to parents of children with disabilities, their professional partners, and their communities. The Federation is committed to listening to and learning from families, and encouraging full participation in community life by all people — especially those with disabilities.

- 📞 [800-331-0688](tel:+18003310688)
- ✉️ [info@fcsn.org](mailto:info@fcsn.org)
- 🌐 [fcsn.org](https://fcsn.org/)

## MA Division for Children & Youth with Special Health Needs

The Division for Children & Youth with Special Health Needs at the Massachusetts Department of Public Health works with families, providers, and others to support children and youth with special health needs ages **birth to 22** and their families. This includes children and youth with chronic medical, physical, developmental, behavioral, or emotional conditions.

- 📞 Community Support Line: [800-882-1435](tel:+18008821435)
- 🌐 [mass.gov/orgs/division-for-children-youth-with-special-health-needs](https://www.mass.gov/orgs/division-for-children-youth-with-special-health-needs)

## Parents Helping Parents

Does parenting leave you feeling stressed, alone, or overwhelmed? Any parent feeling overwhelmed, isolated, or stressed who would like **free, confidential, and anonymous** support may call. **All languages available.**

- 📞 [800-632-8188](tel:+18006328188) — Parental Stress Line
- 🌐 [parentshelpingparents.org](https://parentshelpingparents.org/)

en.description: Grief support programs for adults, children, and teens — from local Massachusetts groups to national bereavement camps and counseling networks.

content.markdown:
A directory of grief support resources for adults, children, and teens — including Massachusetts-based programs, national organizations, and free bereavement camps.

## For adults

### Mass General Bereavement Support Group

Open to patients and employees of the Mass General community. An **8-week group** for people who have experienced the death of a loved one within the past 1½ years. The fee is covered by most insurances and Medicare.

For any questions, to refer, or to schedule a pre-group screening interview, contact the group leaders Ellen McCarthy, LICSW, or Carol McSheffrey, LICSW:

- 📞 [617-724-8021](tel:+16177248021)

### Association of Death Education & Counseling

Their website provides online resources for coping with loss. The organization can make referrals to support groups throughout the United States.

- 📞 [847-509-0403](tel:+18475090403)

### The Compassionate Friends

Organization dedicated to assisting families toward positive resolution of grief following the death of a child of any age, and to providing information to help others be supportive. Chapters located across the United States and internationally.

- 📞 [877-969-0010](tel:+18779690010)

### Hospice Foundation of America

Offers support and education about death, illness, and the process of bereavement — for those grieving personally or professionally. Provides referrals to grief support groups throughout the United States and sponsors an annual *"Living with Grief"* teleconference series, a monthly bereavement newsletter, and other publications.

- 📞 [800-854-3402](tel:+18008543402)

## For children and teens

### Club STAR: Sharing Together and Remembering

A group for ages **5–18 and their parents** grieving the death of a parent or sibling. Meets 5:30 – 7:30 pm on the first Wednesday of October–June at Mass General Hospital. Organized by Mass General for Children, Child Life Services, and the Social Work Department.

To register, contact Hillary D'Amato, MS, CCLS:
- 📞 [617-643-9276](tel:+16176439276)
- ✉️ [mghclubstar@partners.org](mailto:mghclubstar@partners.org)

### Camp Angel Wings

Developed for children and teens (**6–15 years**) who share similar experiences with grief. The camp provides an educational, therapeutic experience that is also enjoyable, helping to counter the sense of isolation that can follow losing a loved one. Activities like swimming, focused arts and crafts, and small discussion groups help children and teens explore their thoughts and feelings about grief.

- 📞 [508-973-3426](tel:+15089733426)
- ✉️ [campangelwings@southcoast.org](mailto:campangelwings@southcoast.org)
- 🌐 [https://athome.southcoast.org/angel-wings-retreat/](https://athome.southcoast.org/angel-wings-retreat/)

### Camp Erin Boston

A **free**, weekend bereavement camp for youth (**6–17**) grieving the death of a significant person. Combines grief education and emotional support with fun, traditional camp activities. Led by bereavement professionals and caring volunteers, campers explore their grief, learn essential coping skills, and make friends with peers who are also grieving.

Eluna partners with bereavement programs in local communities to fund and grow Camp Erin nationwide. The Boston-area provider is Beth Israel Lahey Health at Home — Watertown (home to the HEARTplay children's bereavement program).

- 📞 [508-309-5107](tel:+15083095107)
- 🌐 [camperinboston.org](https://www.camperinboston.org/)

### Camp Kangaroo

A free weekend retreat providing a camp experience and supportive atmosphere for children (**5–13**) who have experienced the loss of a loved one in the last two years. Participants receive grief education and emotional support combined with fun camp activities that help them learn effective coping strategies.

- 📞 Luisa Kcomt: [847-692-1000](tel:+18476921000)
- ✉️ [LKcomt@Seasons.org](mailto:LKcomt@Seasons.org)
- 🌐 [seasonsfoundation.org/camp-kangaroo](http://seasonsfoundation.org/camp-kangaroo)

### Care Dimensions

The most comprehensive grief support program in Massachusetts. Licensed bereavement counselors offer support groups and workshops for anyone who has experienced a death. Individual counseling is also offered to people grieving the death of a loved one who was on Care Dimensions hospice service.

Services include individual consultation and referrals, workshops and support groups, bereavement resources, community education programs, and remembrance and tribute programs. The children's program provides specialized support for children and teens, including **Camp Stepping Stones**, their summer family retreat.

- 📞 [855-774-5100](tel:+18557745100)
- ✉️ [Grief@CareDimensions.org](mailto:Grief@CareDimensions.org)
- 🌐 [caredimensions.org/grief-support](https://www.caredimensions.org/grief-support/)

### Comfort Zone Camp

A bereavement camp for children (**7–17**) who have lost a sibling, parent, or primary caregiver. **Free of charge**, with confidence-building activities and age-based support groups. Programs are also offered to families, plus young adult programs for ages 18–25.

Held year-round across the country; primary locations are California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, North Carolina, and Virginia (HQ).

- 📞 [804-377-3430](tel:+18043773430)
- ✉️ [info@comfortzonecamp.org](mailto:info@comfortzonecamp.org)
- 🌐 [comfortzonecamp.org/programs](https://comfortzonecamp.org/programs/)

### HEARTplay Program

CareGroup Parmenter's award-winning bereavement program for children, teens, and young adults who have experienced a death. Through conversation, music, movement, visual expression, writing, and storytelling, participants share their feelings and experiences.

Groups are **free of charge** through grants and donations. Offered monthly or bi-monthly in Wayland, MA and Newton, MA. Registration is required.

- 📞 Jennifer Wiles: [508-309-5107](tel:+15083095107)
- 🌐 [heartplayprogram.org](https://www.heartplayprogram.org/contact)

### The Carriage House — Seven Hills Foundation

A grief support center for children ages **3–18** and their families. The only program in Central Massachusetts providing children and teens a space to grieve the death of a loved one alongside peers also experiencing grief and loss.

The first step is a telephone intake, then an orientation session at The Carriage House. Families complete paperwork and are assigned to age-appropriate peer groups as space is available.

- 📞 [508-753-5425 ext. 6430](tel:+15087535425)
- 🌐 [sevenhills.org/programs/grief-support](https://www.sevenhills.org/programs/grief-support)

### The Center for Hope & Healing

Compassionate, individualized grief support for any stage. Offers an expansive grief support group program plus community programs like **Camp BraveHeart** for kids, as well as remembrance events. Services are offered throughout Rhode Island and Massachusetts.

- 📞 [888-528-9077](tel:+18885289077)
- 🌐 [hopehealthco.org/services/hospice-care/grief-support](https://www.hopehealthco.org/services/hospice-care/grief-support/)

### The Children's Room

Creates safe, supportive communities so that no child, teen, or family has to grieve alone. Offers hope and healing to children and teens **3½ to 18** who have experienced the death of a parent or sibling. Parents and caregivers also have opportunities to meet, talk about parenting a grieving child, and give and receive support.

Services include ongoing peer support groups, educational series for parents, teen programming, monthly arts-based family nights, and adult consultations. **All services are provided free of charge.**

- 📞 [781-641-4741](tel:+17816414741)
- ✉️ [info@childrensroom.org](mailto:info@childrensroom.org)
- 🌐 [childrensroom.org](https://childrensroom.org/)

### The Garden: A Center for Grieving Children and Teens

Support to grieving young people and their families following the death of someone close — parents, siblings, other family members, or friends. Programs and discussion groups help young people identify and share their feelings and begin the healing process. Parents and guardians meet separately for a chance to discuss their own concerns.

The Garden runs **two programs annually** at its Northampton location: an 8-week session in the fall and a 10-week session in the spring. Services are also increasingly accessible through area schools.

- 📞 Shelly Bathe Lenn: [413-582-5312](tel:+14135825312)
- ✉️ [slenn@cooleydickinson.org](mailto:slenn@cooleydickinson.org)
- 🌐 [https://www.mightycause.com/organization/Thegarden](https://www.mightycause.com/organization/Thegarden/)

### Good Grief Program — Boston Medical Center

Comprehensive consultation for caregivers supporting grieving children after a significant loss (death, divorce, or separation from a primary caregiver). Offers grief-sensitive training and consultation for educators, schools, and other community agencies, and connects individuals to grief resources and referrals. **Spanish-speaking counselors available.**

- 📞 [617-414-4005](tel:+16174144005)
- ✉️ Maureen Patterson-Feder: [Maureen.Patterson@bmc.org](mailto:Maureen.Patterson@bmc.org)
- ✉️ Minelia Rodriguez: [minelia.rodriguez@bmc.org](mailto:minelia.rodriguez@bmc.org)
- 🌐 [bmc.org/programs/good-grief-program](https://www.bmc.org/programs/good-grief-program)

### Rick's Place

Supports children, teens (**5–18**), and their families after a loved one has died. Through facilitated peer support groups, Rick's Place offers grieving children and their caregivers a safe place to remember their loved ones and honor their memories — avoiding the isolation such a loss can produce.

- 📞 [423-279-2010](tel:+14232792010)
- 🌐 [ricksplacema.org/grief-support-services](https://ricksplacema.org/grief-support-services/)

### Wildflower Camp Foundation

Offers scholarship assistance for summer camp and enrichment programs to families in which **a parent has died**. The experience provides restoration for both children and the surviving parent. Summers are the most challenging time for single-parent families; the carefree summer days, new friends, and break from pain at home are an invaluable experience for grieving children and a much-needed respite for the surviving parent.

- 📞 [781-861-1413](tel:+17818611413)
- ✉️ [info@wildflowercampfoundation.org](mailto:info@wildflowercampfoundation.org)
- 🌐 [wildflowercampfoundation.org](https://www.wildflowercampfoundation.org)

---

> This is not a full list of resources available to you and your family. If you have questions about the resources listed or would like more information about bereavement support, please contact the Mass General Hospital Social Work Department: 📞 [617-726-2643](tel:+16177262643).

Offers support and education about death, illness, and the process of bereavement — for those grieving personally or professionally. Provides referrals to grief support groups throughout the United States and sponsors an annual *"Living with Grief"* teleconference series, a monthly bereavement newsletter, and other publications.

- 📞 [800-854-3402](tel:+18008543402)

### Club STAR: Sharing Together and Remembering

A group for ages **5–18 and their parents** grieving the death of a parent or sibling. Meets 5:30 – 7:30 pm on the first Wednesday of October–June at Mass General Hospital. Organized by Mass General for Children, Child Life Services, and the Social Work Department.

To register, contact Hillary D'Amato, MS, CCLS:
- 📞 [617-643-9276](tel:+16176439276)
- ✉️ [mghclubstar@partners.org](mailto:mghclubstar@partners.org)

### Camp Angel Wings

Developed for children and teens (**6–15 years**) who share similar experiences with grief. The camp provides an educational, therapeutic experience that is also enjoyable, helping to counter the sense of isolation that can follow losing a loved one. Activities like swimming, focused arts and crafts, and small discussion groups help children and teens explore their thoughts and feelings about grief.

- 📞 [508-973-3426](tel:+15089733426)
- ✉️ [campangelwings@southcoast.org](mailto:campangelwings@southcoast.org)
- 🌐 [https://athome.southcoast.org/angel-wings-retreat/](https://athome.southcoast.org/angel-wings-retreat/)

### Camp Erin Boston

A **free**, weekend bereavement camp for youth (**6–17**) grieving the death of a significant person. Combines grief education and emotional support with fun, traditional camp activities. Led by bereavement professionals and caring volunteers, campers explore their grief, learn essential coping skills, and make friends with peers who are also grieving.

Eluna partners with bereavement programs in local communities to fund and grow Camp Erin nationwide. The Boston-area provider is Beth Israel Lahey Health at Home — Watertown (home to the HEARTplay children's bereavement program).

- 📞 [508-309-5107](tel:+15083095107)
- 🌐 [camperinboston.org](https://www.camperinboston.org/)

### Camp Kangaroo

A free weekend retreat providing a camp experience and supportive atmosphere for children (**5–13**) who have experienced the loss of a loved one in the last two years. Participants receive grief education and emotional support combined with fun camp activities that help them learn effective coping strategies.

- 📞 Luisa Kcomt: [847-692-1000](tel:+18476921000)
- ✉️ [LKcomt@Seasons.org](mailto:LKcomt@Seasons.org)
- 🌐 [seasonsfoundation.org/camp-kangaroo](http://seasonsfoundation.org/camp-kangaroo)

### Care Dimensions

The most comprehensive grief support program in Massachusetts. Licensed bereavement counselors offer support groups and workshops for anyone who has experienced a death. Individual counseling is also offered to people grieving the death of a loved one who was on Care Dimensions hospice service.

Services include individual consultation and referrals, workshops and support groups, bereavement resources, community education programs, and remembrance and tribute programs. The children's program provides specialized support for children and teens, including **Camp Stepping Stones**, their summer family retreat.

- 📞 [855-774-5100](tel:+18557745100)
- ✉️ [Grief@CareDimensions.org](mailto:Grief@CareDimensions.org)
- 🌐 [caredimensions.org/grief-support](https://www.caredimensions.org/grief-support/)

### Comfort Zone Camp

A bereavement camp for children (**7–17**) who have lost a sibling, parent, or primary caregiver. **Free of charge**, with confidence-building activities and age-based support groups. Programs are also offered to families, plus young adult programs for ages 18–25.

Held year-round across the country; primary locations are California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, North Carolina, and Virginia (HQ).

- 📞 [804-377-3430](tel:+18043773430)
- ✉️ [info@comfortzonecamp.org](mailto:info@comfortzonecamp.org)
- 🌐 [comfortzonecamp.org/programs](https://comfortzonecamp.org/programs/)

### HEARTplay Program

CareGroup Parmenter's award-winning bereavement program for children, teens, and young adults who have experienced a death. Through conversation, music, movement, visual expression, writing, and storytelling, participants share their feelings and experiences.

Groups are **free of charge** through grants and donations. Offered monthly or bi-monthly in Wayland, MA and Newton, MA. Registration is required.

- 📞 Jennifer Wiles: [508-309-5107](tel:+15083095107)
- 🌐 [heartplayprogram.org](https://www.heartplayprogram.org/contact)

### The Carriage House — Seven Hills Foundation

A grief support center for children ages **3–18** and their families. The only program in Central Massachusetts providing children and teens a space to grieve the death of a loved one alongside peers also experiencing grief and loss.

The first step is a telephone intake, then an orientation session at The Carriage House. Families complete paperwork and are assigned to age-appropriate peer groups as space is available.

- 📞 [508-753-5425 ext. 6430](tel:+15087535425)
- 🌐 [sevenhills.org/programs/grief-support](https://www.sevenhills.org/programs/grief-support)

### The Center for Hope & Healing

Compassionate, individualized grief support for any stage. Offers an expansive grief support group program plus community programs like **Camp BraveHeart** for kids, as well as remembrance events. Services are offered throughout Rhode Island and Massachusetts.

- 📞 [888-528-9077](tel:+18885289077)
- 🌐 [hopehealthco.org/services/hospice-care/grief-support](https://www.hopehealthco.org/services/hospice-care/grief-support/)

### The Children's Room

Creates safe, supportive communities so that no child, teen, or family has to grieve alone. Offers hope and healing to children and teens **3½ to 18** who have experienced the death of a parent or sibling. Parents and caregivers also have opportunities to meet, talk about parenting a grieving child, and give and receive support.

Services include ongoing peer support groups, educational series for parents, teen programming, monthly arts-based family nights, and adult consultations. **All services are provided free of charge.**

- 📞 [781-641-4741](tel:+17816414741)
- ✉️ [info@childrensroom.org](mailto:info@childrensroom.org)
- 🌐 [childrensroom.org](https://childrensroom.org/)

### The Garden: A Center for Grieving Children and Teens

Support to grieving young people and their families following the death of someone close — parents, siblings, other family members, or friends. Programs and discussion groups help young people identify and share their feelings and begin the healing process. Parents and guardians meet separately for a chance to discuss their own concerns.

The Garden runs **two programs annually** at its Northampton location: an 8-week session in the fall and a 10-week session in the spring. Services are also increasingly accessible through area schools.

- 📞 Shelly Bathe Lenn: [413-582-5312](tel:+14135825312)
- ✉️ [slenn@cooleydickinson.org](mailto:slenn@cooleydickinson.org)
- 🌐 [https://www.mightycause.com/organization/Thegarden](https://www.mightycause.com/organization/Thegarden/)

### Good Grief Program — Boston Medical Center

Comprehensive consultation for caregivers supporting grieving children after a significant loss (death, divorce, or separation from a primary caregiver). Offers grief-sensitive training and consultation for educators, schools, and other community agencies, and connects individuals to grief resources and referrals. **Spanish-speaking counselors available.**

- 📞 [617-414-4005](tel:+16174144005)
- ✉️ Maureen Patterson-Feder: [Maureen.Patterson@bmc.org](mailto:Maureen.Patterson@bmc.org)
- ✉️ Minelia Rodriguez: [minelia.rodriguez@bmc.org](mailto:minelia.rodriguez@bmc.org)
- 🌐 [bmc.org/programs/good-grief-program](https://www.bmc.org/programs/good-grief-program)

### Rick's Place

Supports children, teens (**5–18**), and their families after a loved one has died. Through facilitated peer support groups, Rick's Place offers grieving children and their caregivers a safe place to remember their loved ones and honor their memories — avoiding the isolation such a loss can produce.

- 📞 [423-279-2010](tel:+14232792010)
- 🌐 [ricksplacema.org/grief-support-services](https://ricksplacema.org/grief-support-services/)

### Wildflower Camp Foundation

Offers scholarship assistance for summer camp and enrichment programs to families in which **a parent has died**. The experience provides restoration for both children and the surviving parent. Summers are the most challenging time for single-parent families; the carefree summer days, new friends, and break from pain at home are an invaluable experience for grieving children and a much-needed respite for the surviving parent.

- 📞 [781-861-1413](tel:+17818611413)
- ✉️ [info@wildflowercampfoundation.org](mailto:info@wildflowercampfoundation.org)
- 🌐 [wildflowercampfoundation.org](https://www.wildflowercampfoundation.org)

title: Breastfeeding: Getting Started

en.description: How to latch, hand express, and pump — plus how to tell whether your baby is getting enough milk.

content.markdown:
Breastfeeding is a skill, and most parents need practice and help to get comfortable with it. The short videos and guides below cover the basics: how to position your baby, how to get a good latch, how to express milk by hand or with a pump, and how to tell that your baby is feeding well.

If something isn't working, that is normal and it is worth asking for help early. Ask your nurse or care team to connect you with a lactation consultant.

title: Who’s Who on the PICU Team

en.description: A guide to every role on your child's PICU care team, what they do, and how they support your family.

content.markdown:
## Physicians (MD)

The Physicians on the unit consist of Attendings, Fellows, Residents, and Medical Students. Please see the “Critical Care Doctors” link on the app to learn more about the different roles of the medical team. 

## Nurses (RN)

The RNs on the PICU work 12-hour shifts, either from 7a-7p or 7p-7a. Your child’s Nursing Team provides high-level clinical care while managing the unique physical, emotional, and developmental needs of patients, often acting as a bridge between physicians, patients, and families. 

## Patient Care Assistants (PCA)

The PCAs on the PICU work in 4-, 8-, or 12-hour increments, both day and night. PCAs provide around-the-clock care to patients under the supervision of a nurse.

## Respiratory Therapists (RT)

RTs evaluate, treat, and care for patients with breathing or cardiopulmonary disorders, ranging from asthma to chronic lung diseases and emergency trauma. There is an RT present on the PICU 24 hours a day.

## Child Life Specialist (CLS)

CLS’s are trained to work with children in medical settings, using play and developmental interventions to help children and families adjust to, and understand, their experience in the hospital.

## Art Therapy

Art therapy uses simple art activities to help patients express themselves and develop a sense of well-being through the creative process. You do not have to be an artist to enjoy and take advantage of art’s powers to enhance wellness.

## Music Therapy

Music therapy can help support a child’s experience through active music making, gentle live music for relaxation, music-supported meditation, and much more.

## Pet Therapy

Specially trained dogs who visit your hospital room to help children cope and overcome the stress that they may experience during their stay. Ask your Child Life Specialist about our pet therapy schedule.

## Social Work (SW)

SW is available to discuss new diagnoses as well as the crisis of hospitalization and family adjustment to hospitalization. SW can help support your child and family throughout the entire hospital stay.

## Case Management (CM)

To ensure that patients are receiving the services they need to achieve an optimum quality of life, the CM coordinates treatments and providers, facilitates safe transitions between hospital and outpatient settings and educates patients, families and providers on best health practices and services in the outpatient setting.

## Spiritual Care (SC)

As partners in healing, SC Providers serve patients, families, visitors and staff through comfort, encouragement and prayer. They embrace life-long learning, respect the dignity and worth of every person, and honor the sacredness of the human spirit. SC services are always free, private and confidential.

## Physical Therapy (PT)

Specialize in focusing on the large motor groups that contribute to walking, reaching, standing, and many more physical activities.

## Occupational Therapy (OT)

Offer skilled treatment to help individuals achieve independence in all facets of their lives. OT facilitates early mobility, sensory regulation, and developmental support to improve recovery.

## Speech-Language Pathologists (SLP)

Assess, diagnose, treat, and help to prevent communication and swallowing disorders in patients.

## Nutritionists/Dieticians

Trained to care for children with a variety of feeding difficulties. Nutritionists work together with the Dietary team to provide tailored nutritional care that helps support growth, development, and health management.

title: Parking at Mass General

en.description: Where to park, what it costs with validation, and where to get your ticket validated — there are no cashiers at the exits.

content.markdown:
Massachusetts General Hospital's main campus spans nearly 30 buildings. We offer parking for patients and visitors at:

- Charles River Plaza
- Fruit Street Garage
- Parkman Street Garage
- Yawkey Center

We also offer valet parking at the Wang and Yawkey Centers.

For additional information about parking rates at Mass General, please contact the Parking Office.

### Mass General Parking Office

- 📞 [617-726-8886](tel:+16177268886)
- 🌐 [massgeneralbrigham.org/en/patients-visitors/visitor-information/plan-visit/directions-parking](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/en/patients-visitors/visitor-information/plan-visit/directions-parking)

## Get your ticket validated

Parking tickets are validated at the cashier in the central payment office, located on the ground floor lobby of each garage. Please note there are no cashiers at the garage exits.

- The Yawkey Center cashier office is open from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. every day. Tickets can be processed in Fruit Street Garage after hours.
- The Parkman Street Garage cashier office is open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. from Monday to Friday. It's closed on weekends and holidays. Tickets can be processed in Fruit Street Garage cashier office.

## Validated patient and visitor rates

New rates effective February 1, 2026, at the Fruit Street, Parkman Street, Yawkey Center and Charles River Plaza garages:

- 0 to 30 minutes: Free
- 30 minutes to 1 hour: $11
- 1 to 2 hours: $12
- 2 to 4 hours: $14
- 4 to 6 hours: $16
- 6 to 8 hours: $19
- 8 to 24 hours: $21

Without validation, parking costs up to $65 a day.

## Appointments at 165, 175, or 185 Cambridge Street

Patients with appointments at 165, 175, and 185 Cambridge Street should park in the Charles River Plaza garage, with the entrance at 207 Cambridge Street, next to Flour Bakery. Parking on the outside deck is for Charles River Plaza (CRP) retail customers only.

Patients must have their parking ticket validated by the cashier in the 165 Cambridge Street lobby, or at the garage cashier office located to the right of the garage exit. Patient validation is not available at the exit lane parking equipment.

### Charles River Plaza Garage

Entrance next to Flour Bakery.

- 207 Cambridge Street, Boston, MA 02114

title: Getting Here by Public Transit

en.description: The hospital is across the street from the Red Line — often easier than parking downtown.

content.markdown:
Due to our high volume of visitors every day, we recommend that you use public transportation whenever possible. We are located directly across the street from the **Charles/MGH stop on the MBTA Red Line** and a short walk from the Bowdoin (Blue Line) and North Station (Green and Orange Line) stations.

North Station also has commuter rail.

If you do drive, see *Parking at Mass General* for garages, validation, and rates.

content.markdown:
## Guest Wi-Fi

Visitors have access to a wireless Internet connection throughout most of our campuses:

- Guest network: **PHSPIAGUEST**
- No password required

You'll be asked to accept Mass General Brigham's [Acceptable Use Policy](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/en/patients-visitors/visitor-information/plan-visit/wifi-use-policy) to connect.

The guest network is not secure, but it does provide content filtering.

## Charging your devices

Visitors must use their own laptop or mobile device to connect to the wireless network. We provide several charging stations throughout our campuses. Please ask the care team before plugging a laptop or mobile device into an outlet.

title: Journal Writing to Manage Stress

en.description: Writing in a journal can help release worries and ease stress during a PICU stay. Learn the benefits and find prompts to get started.

content.markdown:
## Benefits of journal writing

When you are coping with challenges, writing your thoughts and feelings in a journal can help you express those unspoken thoughts and release some of your worries.

Journal writing can also help you record what happened on a given day. It allows you to reflect on the events at a later date. Rereading your journal gives you the chance to review, process and share information with family members.

Research has shown that people who wrote in a journal while in an intensive care setting (such as the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit, or PICU) had less stress and a better sense of well-being.

The video below shares more about the MGHfC Journal Program and how it can help you during your PICU stay.

content.caption: About the FAC Journal Program at MGHfC — Mass General Brigham for Children

content.markdown:
## Writing prompts for adults and families

Writing in a journal is a great way to express yourself, cope with stress and explore your feelings and experiences. Here are some writing prompts to get you started. Feel free to use the prompts in any order or pick your favorites.

### Just get started

- Just write! Put pen to paper and write. Write anything. Do not lift your hand off the paper. If you need to write “Just write” over and over, do so. Before long, your thoughts will emerge and you will write them down.
- Finish this sentence: “I remember when…” Write as many responses to the prompt as you would like. This can help you recall old or favorite memories and get your thoughts flowing.

### Use your senses

- What colors do you see?
- What sounds do you hear?

### What do you love?

- Ask yourself, “If I could be anywhere right now, where would I be?”
- Write about this thought: “I feel the most free when…”
- What do you like to do on weekends?
- What new activities would you like to try? (Such as yoga, dance, dog walking, reading, going to movies or others.)
- What activities are comforting for you? (Such as writing in a journal, walking in the woods, listening to music, gathering shells on a beach or others.)

### Remember good memories

- What was your most memorable trip?
- What activities did you like to do in the summer when you were a child?
- What is your favorite memory with a grandparent, parent, sibling, teacher, coach or mentor?

### Feel the love from friends and family

- Who gives you comfort and support, and why? A family member? A longtime friend?
- Remember, “How do my best friends make me feel when I’m with them?”
- Ask yourself, “When I’m with my (fill in the blank, such as a grandmother) I feel really loved because…”
- Who was (and perhaps still is) your best childhood friend?

### Find inspiration from others

- “Courage is found in unlikely places.” — J. R. R. Tolkien
- “I’ve been searching for ways to heal myself, and I’ve found that kindness is the best way.” — Lady Gaga
- “What lies behind us and what lies before us are tiny matters compared to what lies within us.” — Often credited to Oliver Wendell Holmes
- “You are braver than you believe, stronger than you seem and smarter than you think.” — Christopher Robin, in Disney’s Pooh’s Grand Adventure (1997)

## I want to talk to someone about the feelings that come up when I write. What can I do?

If you would like support for the feelings that may come up as you write, ask your care team to page Social Work, Child Life Services or Spiritual Care at MGHfC.

description.en: Writing in a journal can help release worries and ease stress during a PICU stay. Learn the benefits and find prompts to get started.

markdown.en:
When you are coping with challenges, writing your thoughts and feelings in a journal can help you express those unspoken thoughts and release some of your worries.

Journal writing can also help you record what happened on a given day. It allows you to reflect on the events at a later date. Rereading your journal gives you the chance to review, process and share information with family members.

Research has shown that people who wrote in a journal while in an intensive care setting (such as the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit, or PICU) had less stress and a better sense of well-being.

The video below shares more about the MGHfC Journal Program and how it can help you during your PICU stay.

title.en: Writing prompts for adults and families

markdown.en:
Writing in a journal is a great way to express yourself, cope with stress and explore your feelings and experiences. Here are some writing prompts to get you started. Feel free to use the prompts in any order or pick your favorites.

### Just get started

- Just write! Put pen to paper and write. Write anything. Do not lift your hand off the paper. If you need to write “Just write” over and over, do so. Before long, your thoughts will emerge and you will write them down.
- Finish this sentence: “I remember when…” Write as many responses to the prompt as you would like. This can help you recall old or favorite memories and get your thoughts flowing.

### Use your senses

- What colors do you see?
- What sounds do you hear?

### What do you love?

- Ask yourself, “If I could be anywhere right now, where would I be?”
- Write about this thought: “I feel the most free when…”
- What do you like to do on weekends?
- What new activities would you like to try? (Such as yoga, dance, dog walking, reading, going to movies or others.)
- What activities are comforting for you? (Such as writing in a journal, walking in the woods, listening to music, gathering shells on a beach or others.)

### Remember good memories

- What was your most memorable trip?
- What activities did you like to do in the summer when you were a child?
- What is your favorite memory with a grandparent, parent, sibling, teacher, coach or mentor?

### Feel the love from friends and family

- Who gives you comfort and support, and why? A family member? A longtime friend?
- Remember, “How do my best friends make me feel when I’m with them?”
- Ask yourself, “When I’m with my (fill in the blank, such as a grandmother) I feel really loved because…”
- Who was (and perhaps still is) your best childhood friend?

### Find inspiration from others

- “Courage is found in unlikely places.” — J. R. R. Tolkien
- “I’ve been searching for ways to heal myself, and I’ve found that kindness is the best way.” — Lady Gaga
- “What lies behind us and what lies before us are tiny matters compared to what lies within us.” — Often credited to Oliver Wendell Holmes
- “You are braver than you believe, stronger than you seem and smarter than you think.” — Christopher Robin, in Disney’s Pooh’s Grand Adventure (1997)

title: Journal Writing Prompts for Teens Age 13 and Older

en.description: Writing prompts for teens to express themselves, cope with stress and explore their feelings and experiences in a journal.

content.markdown:
Writing in a journal is a great way to express yourself, cope with stress and explore your feelings and experiences. Here are some writing prompts to get you started. Feel free to do the prompts in any order or pick your favorites.

## Name your favorites

- What songs are on your favorite playlist?
- What was your favorite childhood book?
- What is it about your favorite activity (such as biking, listening to music, playing basketball, picking up shells on a beach) that makes you feel good?

## Go on an adventure

- What was your greatest childhood adventure?
- What do you like to do on weekends?
- Ask yourself, “If I could be anywhere right now, where would I be?”
- Write about this experience: “I feel the most free when…”

## Try something new

- What new activities would you like to try? (Such as yoga, dancing, dog walking, playing the guitar and others.)

## Feel the love from friends and family

- Who is your best childhood friend and why?
- Write about this experience: “How do my best friends make me feel when I’m with them?”
- Ask yourself, “When I’m with my (fill in the blank, such as your grandmother) I feel really loved because…”

## Find inspiration from other writers

Choose a quote from the list below. You can also find your own quotes from your favorite books, movies or websites. Write your thoughts about the quote. There are no right or wrong responses.

### Quotes from the Harry Potter series

- “It is our choices, Harry, that show what we really are, far more than our abilities.” — Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets by J.K. Rowling
- “Words are, in my not-so-humble opinion, our most inexhaustible source of magic.” — Albus Dumbledore
- “I solemnly swear I’m up to no good!” — Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban by J.K. Rowling

### Quotes from other writers and artists

- “Be who you are and say what you feel because those who mind don’t matter and those who matter don’t mind.” — Often credited to Dr. Seuss
- “Be yourself. Everyone else is taken.” — Oscar Wilde
- “You’re braver than you believe, stronger than you seem, and smarter than you think.” — Christopher Robin, in Disney’s Pooh’s Grand Adventure (1997)
- “However small the chance might be of striking it lucky, the chance was there.” — Charlie and the Chocolate Factory by Roald Dahl
- “You can’t stop the waves but you can learn to surf.” — Wherever You Go, There You Are by Jon Kabat-Zinn
- “Only that day dawns to which we are awake.” — Walden by Henry David Thoreau
- “What lies behind us and what lies before us are tiny matters compared to what lies within us.” — Often credited to Oliver Wendell Holmes
- “Courage is found in unlikely places.” — J. R. R. Tolkien
- “I’ve been searching for ways to heal myself, and I’ve found that kindness is the best way.” — Lady Gaga

## Learn about the journal program

The video below shares more about the MGHfC Journal Program and how it can help you during your PICU stay.

title: Lactation Support Program

en.description: The Lactation Support Program helps manage breastfeeding challenges. Find support for your breastfeeding goals.

content.markdown:
You do not have to figure breastfeeding out alone. Ask your nurse or care team to connect you with a lactation consultant while you are here.

Our outpatient clinic sees mothers of breastfeeding babies, regardless of where you gave birth.

Outpatient care is available through a breastfeeding and lactation medicine clinic, which provides medical care for more complex feeding concerns. This clinic is designed for patients who may need a higher level of evaluation and treatment. Visits are billed as medical appointments.

### Lactation Support Program

- 📞 [617-724-2229](tel:+16177242229) (Massachusetts General Hospital)
- 🌐 [massgeneralbrigham.org/en/services/lactation-support](https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/en/services/lactation-support)

title: Discharge Readiness Checklist

en.description: A checklist to help you get ready to take your child home: medicines, follow-up care, insurance, school and home.

content.markdown:
### Discharge readiness checklist

Work through this at your pace. Bring anything you can't check off to your care team.

#### Medications & supplies

- [ ] I know each medicine's name, dose, and what it's for
- [ ] I have written instructions and a schedule
- [ ] Prescriptions are filled or on the way
- [ ] I have any needed supplies (syringes, feeding pump, oxygen, etc.)
- [ ] I know what side effects should prompt a call

#### Follow-up care

- [ ] PCP follow-up scheduled (within 1–2 weeks)
- [ ] Subspecialist follow-ups scheduled (or on the calendar to book)
- [ ] I know what number to call if something changes
- [ ] Records will be sent to our PCP and outside providers

#### Insurance & school

- [ ] Insurance approval confirmed for meds and equipment
- [ ] School / daycare paperwork completed (return-to-school note, activity restrictions)
- [ ] 504 plan or IEP updates requested if needed

#### Home readiness

- [ ] Home has heat, food, transportation for follow-ups
- [ ] I know who to call for financial or resource help
- [ ] Rehab, LTAC, or home nursing arranged (if applicable)
- [ ] Mental health follow-up in place for the patient or family (if needed)

es.description: Una lista para ayudarle a prepararse para llevar a su hijo a casa: medicamentos, atención de seguimiento, seguro médico, escuela y hogar.

content.markdown:
### Lista de preparación para el alta

Vaya a su propio ritmo. Hable con su equipo de atención sobre todo lo que todavía no pueda marcar.

#### Medicamentos y suministros

- [ ] Sé el nombre y la dosis de cada medicamento, y para qué sirve
- [ ] Tengo instrucciones por escrito y un horario
- [ ] Las recetas están surtidas o en camino
- [ ] Tengo los suministros necesarios (jeringas, bomba de alimentación, oxígeno, etc.)
- [ ] Sé qué efectos secundarios son motivo para llamar

#### Atención de seguimiento

- [ ] Cita de seguimiento con el pediatra de cabecera programada (en 1 a 2 semanas)
- [ ] Citas de seguimiento con especialistas programadas (o anotadas para pedirlas)
- [ ] Sé a qué número llamar si algo cambia
- [ ] Los expedientes médicos se enviarán a nuestro pediatra de cabecera y a otros proveedores

#### Seguro médico y escuela

- [ ] El seguro aprobó los medicamentos y el equipo
- [ ] Los papeles de la escuela o guardería están completos (nota para volver a la escuela, límites de actividad)
- [ ] Pedimos cambios al plan 504 o al IEP (plan de educación individualizado), si hace falta

#### Preparación del hogar

- [ ] En casa hay calefacción, comida y transporte para las citas de seguimiento
- [ ] Sé a quién llamar para pedir ayuda económica o con otros recursos
- [ ] Rehabilitación, hospital de cuidados prolongados (LTAC) o enfermería en casa organizados (si corresponde)
- [ ] Seguimiento de salud mental organizado para el paciente o la familia (si hace falta)
